Probabilistic Microplastics Risk Characterization: Central California Rivers

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source
Author

Scott Coffin, Ph.D. — California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)

Published

July 30, 2026

1. Overview

This document presents an end-to-end, fully probabilistic environmental risk assessment (ERA) workflow for microplastics in freshwater surface water and sediment from four central California rivers (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo). The workflow proceeds through five steps:

  1. Raw particle data → power-law slope (α) via C-PSD — cumulative particle size distribution fitted using the two-step LOD detection algorithm of Segur et al. (2026).
  2. Monitoring concentrations → probabilistic rescaling — power-law integration converts measurements from a sampled size range to a target range, propagating slope uncertainty via Monte Carlo (Coffin et al. 2022).
  3. Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) — nonparametric bootstrap of corrected site-level concentrations.
  4. Hazard threshold distribution — probabilistic species sensitivity distributions (pSSD++) using the PSSDplusplus R package and ToMEx 2.0 toxicity database.
  5. Risk characterization — Monte Carlo pairing of exposure and hazard distributions, expressed as risk quotient (RQ = Exposure/Hazard) and exceedance probability P(RQ > 1).

All custom R functions (fit_cpsd_segur_r, correction_factor, bootstrap_eed, mc2d_risk, etc.) live in R/mp_risk_utils.R and R/cpsd_plotting.R for reuse and eventual integration into PSSDplusplus. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD-detection algorithm is implemented directly in R/mp_risk_utils.R as pure R.

Methodological basis. This assessment treats the C-PSD slope convention, transport-induced slope structure, sampling depth, polymer density, and water-sediment PSD coherence as explicit, quantified uncertainty sources. Both the exposure-side correction factor and the hazard-side particle-trait alignment inside pSSD++ (length, area, volume, mass) integrate the differential PSD slope (apsd = acpsd − 1), locked by a rendered worked-example assertion in Section 5.1.0 (Koelmans et al. 2020: CF = 8.32 for 30–2000 µm → 1–5000 µm at α = 1.6). Sediment (beach sand) is retained as an illustrative/methods demonstration only and excluded from the headline risk conclusion: its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis, not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement (Section 11). Sediment is additionally framed as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so any single-time-point sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot (Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026; Section 11) — a framing/sensitivity addition, not a re-introduction of sediment into the headline conclusion. The full revision history behind these corrections (prior convention errors and their quantified before/after effect) is in Appendix A and docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md. Results at a glance (river/ocean headline RQ, piecewise bound, sediment exclusion) follows Section 12; the fully quantified executive summary is in Key Findings.

3. Load data

3.1 Raw particle-length observations

This data comes from microscopy/FTIR particle measurements (a table of individual particles).

Show the code 
# import river particle data (includes plastics and non-plastics)
raw_particles <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_comb.rds") |> 
  # filter to only QC-passing particles
  dplyr::filter(!material_class %in% c("mineral", "organic matter"), #filter non-plastic
                acc_analy_conf == "confident", # only use confident spectra
                bad_spectra) %>% #filter out bad spectra
  # extract the first 8-digit block from the ID
  mutate(date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"), date = ymd(date_raw), # convert YYYYMMDD → Date
         shape = case_when(aspect_ratio >= 3 ~ "fiber", # common definition of fiber - check!
                           aspect_ratio <= 3 ~ "fragment"),
         length_um = max_length_um,
         width_um = min_length_um,
         sample_depth_general = recode(sample_depth_general, "depth" = "subsurface")
  ) |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl)

# subset by matrix for downstream analysis
raw_particles_river <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "river water") #river water, ocean water, or beach sand are options

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "ocean water")

raw_particles_river |> 
  group_by(shape) |> 
  summarize(count = n(),
            mean_length = mean(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_length = min(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_length = max(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_length = sd(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_width = mean(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_width = min(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_width = max(width_um, na.rm = TRUE)
            )

3.1.1 Estimate particle volume

Show the code 
# ---- Thickness (height) factor from measured raw data ----
# Kooi et al. (2022) H = r * W, where r is median(W/L). 
ratio_tbl <- raw_particles_river |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1/aspect_ratio,
    # area-derived effective width (rectangle proxy); protects against noisy min_length
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),            # central estimate
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative low
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative high
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# quick sanity check: ratio table + summary of volumes
ratio_tbl

Show the code 
# ---- Volumes ----
# Ellipsoid (Kooi-compatible): V = (pi/6) * L * W * H  with H = r * W
# => V = (pi/6) * r * L * W^2
# Cylinder assumption for fibers: V = pi * (W/2)^2 * L

raw_particles_river <- raw_particles_river |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(# thickness in um (assume L/W = H/W)
    height_um = r_med * width_um) |> 

    mutate(# ellipsoid volume in um^3 (primary; Kooi-consistent)
      V_um3  = case_when(shape == "fragment" ~ (pi/6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
    # fiber cylinder sensitivity in um^3 (only meaningful for fibers)
                        shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um/2)^2 * length_um,
                        TRUE ~ NA_real_)
                        ) |> 
    # estimate particle mass based on volume and polymer-resolved density; retain
    # the legacy fixed-density case as a labeled sensitivity.
    mutate(
      mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
      mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
    )

# export CSV of cleaned up raw particles
write.csv(raw_particles_river, "data_output/Part_dets_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)

raw_particles_river |>
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    V_um3_median = median(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_mean = mean(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_sd = sd(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_median = median(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_mean = mean(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_sd = sd(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Hoffman et al. (2026) identify 3-D geometry and density as higher-priority uncertainty sources than fine differences among settling-velocity equations. Particle density is therefore resolved by broad FTIR polymer class where possible (measured polymer class; density lookup from Hidalgo-Ruz et al. 2012, Table 2), while the legacy fixed 1.1 g/cm^3 case is retained as a sensitivity column. The buoyant/settling flag is an inferred transport category relative to freshwater or seawater density and is used only in the diagnostic Sensitivity section below.

    # recode depth to subsurface

  mutate(Lmin_measured_um = 50,

4. Step 1 — Derive power-law alpha via C-PSD (binned cumulative PSD)

4.1 C-PSD fitting — Segur et al. (2026)

The C-PSD (cumulative particle size distribution) method fits N(≥L) vs L on a log-log scale using binned count data, removing the bin-width bias inherent in the classic BN-PSD approach (Segur et al. 2026). The algorithm is implemented in pure R in R/mp_risk_utils.R as fit_cpsd_segur_r().

Two-step LOD detection algorithm:

  1. Bin particle measurements; compute BN-PSD and C-PSD.
  2. Global OLS on all bins → normalised residuals; retain bins with positive residuals at or above the BN-PSD peak (Low_size ≥ L_max of the BN-PSD).
  3. Exhaustively test all contiguous sub-windows ≥ 3 bins; accept windows with R² ≥ 0.90.
  4. Select the longest accepted window (ties broken by R²) as the fitting range.
  5. OLS on log₁₀ N(≥L) ~ log₁₀ L_low; BN-PSD slope a = a_cpsd − 1.

Method choice: C-PSD is the preferred, robust power-law fitting approach and is not re-litigated in this document. Segur et al. (2026) show that the classic bin-normalized (BN-PSD) method alone is insufficient to correct binning bias, whereas the cumulative C-PSD approach used throughout removes it and returns accuracy comparable to maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE). Our implementation is independently validated: Appendix B confirms it is bit-identical to Segur et al.’s own reference PSD_fit.py code across all nine matrix × shape particle-length PSDs. Segur et al. also note two caveats that motivate the methods-robustness analyses in Section 12.5: the C-PSD right tail slumps where large particles are undercounted, and the method necessarily extrapolates below the measured range, which requires careful fitting-window selection. This section does not fit MLE to justify the C-PSD method choice — that comparison is unnecessary here because Segur et al. (2026) already established C-PSD ≈ MLE in accuracy. A separate, distinct question — how much the risk result (not the method choice) depends on the sub-floor extrapolation model — is tested directly in Section 12.5.2’s model-selection robustness check, which does fit MLE and a tapered/lognormal alternative for that purpose.

4.2 Fit C-PSD to the raw particle data

4.2.1 Particle Length

Show the code 
# Pooled C-PSD fits across all river locations, bin_um = 5 µm
cpsd_fits_river_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_river, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_frag  <- cpsd_fits_river_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_fiber <- cpsd_fits_river_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_all   <- cpsd_fits_river_length$all

The Segur et al. (2026) algorithm fitted power-law slopes of α_CPSD = -2.74 ± 0.04 for fragments (LOD 95 – 350 µm), α_CPSD = -1.67 ± 0.05 for fibers (LOD 175 – 480 µm), and α_CPSD = -1.92 ± 0.04 for all particles pooled (LOD 165 – 385 µm, R² = 0.988). The corresponding differential BN-PSD slopes (a = α_CPSD − 1) are -3.74 (fragment), -2.67 (fiber), and -2.92 (all). For comparison, Segur et al. (2026) report a mean BN-PSD slope of −2.66 ± 0.68 for fragments across ocean and atmosphere samples.

4.2.1.2 Literature comparison of power-law size distribution slopes

The differential BN-PSD slope apsd = acpsd − 1 (equivalent to the negative power-law exponent α in Kooi et al. 2021) characterizes how steeply particle abundance declines with increasing size. Steeper (more negative) apsd values indicate that small particles dominate the count distribution far more strongly than large ones. Comparing this slope across studies and analytical methods provides a critical cross-check on data quality and reveals how sampling methodology shapes the apparent size distribution.

Notation reconciliation. Different publications use different sign conventions. Zhao et al. (2026) and Kooi et al. (2021) report the positive exponent α from the probability density function f(L) ∝ L−α; their α corresponds directly to |apsd| in our Segur notation. Wang et al. (2026) follow the same positive-α convention. Segur et al. (2026) report the negative C-PSD slope acpsd, from which apsd = acpsd − 1.

Power-law size distribution slopes: this study vs. recent literature. All values converted to the BN-PSD differential slope a_psd for comparability.
Source Convention Reported value Equivalent a_psd
This study — fragments (µFTIR, Segur LOD, 95–350 µm) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -2.739 -3.739
This study — fibers (µFTIR, Segur LOD, 175–480 µm) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.671 -2.671
This study — all shapes (µFTIR, Segur LOD, 165–385 µm) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.920 -2.920
Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine/Meuse combined suspended solids (µFTIR) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.650 -3.650
Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine Lobith samples (µFTIR, mean) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.890 -3.890
Wang et al. 2026 — Meuse Eijsden samples (µFTIR, mean) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.190 -3.190
Segur et al. 2026 — ocean reference (C-PSD) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.660 -2.660
Segur et al. 2026 — atmosphere reference (C-PSD) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.550 -2.550
Zhao et al. 2026 — global surface water meta-analysis (45 studies) BN-PSD +α (positive) 1.500 -1.500
Zhao et al. 2026 — mesh-adjusted global surface water BN-PSD +α (positive) 1.530 -1.530
Kooi et al. 2021 — freshwater surface water default BN-PSD +α (positive) 2.640 -2.640
Kooi et al. 2021 — marine surface water default BN-PSD +α (positive) 2.070 -2.070

Key finding — consistency with µFTIR studies, divergence from net-trawl surveys. Our fragment apsd (-3.74) and all-shape apsd (-2.92) are within the range reported by Wang et al. (2026) for Dutch river suspended solids measured by µFTIR (−3.19 to −3.89, mean combined −3.65, SD 0.21). This agreement is not surprising: both datasets use particle-by-particle µFTIR counting on filtered samples. In contrast, our values are substantially steeper than the global surface water meta-analysis compiled by Zhao et al. (2026; mean α = 1.50, equivalent apsd = −1.50, SD 0.53) and the freshwater/marine surface-water defaults reported by Kooi et al. (2021; α = 2.64 freshwater, 2.07 marine). The Segur et al. (2026) reference slopes (ocean −1.66, atmosphere −1.55 in C-PSD notation, equivalent apsd ≈ −2.66 and −2.55) are intermediate.

The divergence from the Zhao/Kooi global averages likely reflects three interacting factors: (1) analytical resolution — µFTIR counting captures particles approaching ~20 µm, whereas most studies in the Zhao meta-analysis used net trawls or pump samples with mesh sizes ≥ 300 µm, systematically missing the numerically dominant small-particle fraction and producing an apparent shallower slope; (2) size range of fit — our Segur LOD algorithm fits the C-PSD over a restricted window (~100–330 µm for fragments) within which the distribution is inherently steeper than a global fit spanning three orders of magnitude; (3) environmental context — California coastal rivers may differ from open-ocean or mixed-environment global compilations.

Fiber vs. fragment. Fibers exhibit a notably shallower slope (apsd = -2.67) than fragments (apsd = -3.74). This is consistent with Zhao et al. (2026), who found that fibers have dramatically lower mesh capture efficiency (0.70% at 330 µm mesh; 37.6% at 20 µm mesh across a 10–5000 µm size range) compared to fragments (7.9% at 330 µm). While our µFTIR pump-and-filter approach avoids the coarsest mesh bias, filter capture of fine fibers (whose short axis — diameter ≤ 10 µm — can pass through a nominal 50 µm pore) may still be lower than for equidimensional fragments. A shallower measured fiber slope would result if fine fibers are under-retained, making observed fiber concentrations a minimum estimate. Users comparing fiber-specific concentrations across studies should be aware of this potential systematic bias.

Implications for data correction. Three recently published correction methodologies were evaluated for applicability to this workflow:

  1. Zhao et al. (2026) — Mesh selectivity correction: This physically-based model corrects for particle loss during mesh-based net trawling or pump filtration. It is not applied here because (a) our particle data derive from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered samples where the Segur LOD algorithm explicitly identifies and corrects for the analytical lower detection limit; (b) the Zhao model is calibrated for net trawls (mesh aperture as the primary parameter) rather than membrane filtration; and (c) our correction_factor() function already accounts for size-range sampling bias through power-law integration, which accomplishes the same conceptual goal. Applying the Zhao correction on top of the existing CF would risk double-counting the lower-size adjustment.

  2. Wang et al. (2026) — µFTIR objective and sieve effects: Wang et al. demonstrated that the 4× µFTIR objective captures only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to the 25× objective (predominantly because the 4× misses sub-50 µm particles). The sieve mesh size (20 µm vs. 5 µm) had minimal effect on size distribution or polymer composition. The present dataset was collected with an approximately 4× objective at 25 µm pixel size, giving a detection floor of ~50 µm. Critically, this floor is already reflected in L_meas_min = 50 µm, and the power-law CF extrapolates particle counts from this floor to 1 µm. The Wang et al. ×33 factor therefore does not apply here — it would double-count the sub-50 µm extrapolation already performed by the CF. A detailed analysis of this intersection and the residual uncertainty in the 50–100 µm marginal detection zone is presented in Section 10.2.

  3. Chen et al. (2026) — Count-to-mass conversion: Chen et al. developed a conditional fragmentation distribution (CFD, Weibull-based) model for converting particle counts to mass, outperforming the simple power-law (CPD) approach. This methodology is not applicable to the present count-based risk assessment workflow (exposure expressed as particles/L); it would be relevant only if mass-based exposure concentrations were required for comparison with mass-normalized ecotoxicological thresholds.

Summary. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD detection and power-law correction workflow remains methodologically consistent for central California riverine monitoring data, and the measured slopes are coherent with other µFTIR-based riverine studies. However, Hoffman et al. (2026) adds a separate unresolved uncertainty: transport-induced PSD distortion can affect the validity of a single-power-law extrapolation and can differ by depth, shape, and polymer buoyancy. The analysis therefore keeps the mesh-selectivity and Wang et al. correction exclusions unchanged, but adds Hoffman sensitivity analyses for slope convention, structural slope uncertainty, depth stratification, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence. The current interpretation is that absolute concentrations are more uncertain than previously stated; the Food Dilution vs. Tissue Translocation ranking is likely robust but is no longer treated as immune to PSD-structure effects.

# Fit C-PSD per river × shape for all three metrics.
# Uses tryCatch to handle sparse data combinations gracefully.
safe_cpsd <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

    fiber    = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5),
    all      = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5)

})

# Helper: extract LOD bounds from a fit object
.lod_bounds <- function(fo) {
  lod_lo <- if (!is.null(fo$lower_lod_used_um) && is.finite(fo$lower_lod_used_um))
               fo$lower_lod_used_um else fo$lower_lod_um
  list(lo = lod_lo, hi = fo$upper_lod_um)
}

# Extract predicted lines + 95% CI ribbon within each fit's valid LOD window
extract_fit_lines <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      if (!is.finite(b$lo) || !is.finite(b$hi) || b$lo >= b$hi) return(NULL)
      grid <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(b$lo, b$hi, length.out = 80))
      pred <- tryCatch(predict(fo$fit, newdata = grid, se.fit = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
      if (is.null(pred)) return(NULL)
      tibble::tibble(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                     L_low    = grid$L_low,
                     logN_fit = pred$fit,
                     logN_lo  = pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit,
                     logN_hi  = pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
    }))
  }))
}

# Extract raw binned data points with an in_lod flag for opacity mapping
extract_fit_points <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$bins)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      fo$bins |>
        dplyr::arrange(L_low) |>
        dplyr::mutate(
          N_ge   = rev(cumsum(rev(n))),
          in_lod = is.finite(b$lo) & is.finite(b$hi) & L_low >= b$lo & L_high <= b$hi
        ) |>
        dplyr::filter(L_low > 0, N_ge > 0) |>
        dplyr::transmute(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                         L_low, logN = log10(N_ge), in_lod)
    }))
  }))
}

4.2.5 Per-river power-law slopes across size metrics

The per-location C-PSD fits from Section 4.2.4 yield a BN-PSD slope apsd for each combination of river location and size metric (length, surface area, volume). Comparing these slopes across metrics shows how the shape of the size distribution changes with the geometric measure used, and whether location-to-location variation is consistent across metrics.

Show the code 
# Extract per-location a_psd for surface area and volume from the per-river fits
extract_loc_slopes <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][["all"]]
    if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
    tibble::tibble(location = loc, a_psd = fo$a_psd, se_a_cpsd = fo$se_a_cpsd, metric = metric_name)
  }))
}

loc_slopes_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(loc_summary, location, a_psd, se_a_cpsd, metric = "Length (µm)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_area, "Surface Area (µm²)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_vol,  "Volume (µm³)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric   = factor(metric, levels = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)")),
    location = factor(location, levels = locations)
  )

# Reference slopes (Segur 2026 ocean mean, length metric)
ref_slopes <- data.frame(
  metric    = factor("Length (µm)", levels = levels(loc_slopes_all$metric)),
  ref_slope = -2.66,
  ref_label = "Segur 2026\nfragment mean"
)

    ggplot2::aes(x = location, y = a_psd, color = location)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(

    width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +

  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = loc_palette, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "River location",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[psd]),
    title    = "BN-PSD slope by river location and size metric",
    subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE  |  Dashed = Segur 2026 fragment reference (length only)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),

cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot

Following the probabilistic rescaling approach (e.g., Coffin et al. 2022), treat the differential PSD slope as uncertain and represent it by a truncated normal distribution. The Segur C-PSD fit estimates acpsd for N(≥L); the Koelmans et al. (2020), Kooi et al. (2021), and Coffin et al. (2022) correction-factor equation integrates dN/dL = k·L^a, so the slope passed to correction_factor() is apsd = acpsd − 1. Hoffman et al. (2026) adds a model-based structural uncertainty concern: transport can produce apparent dual-slope PSDs whose exponents differ by about two, so slope_structural_sd = 0.25 is added as an explicit assumption beyond the fit SE.

Show the code 
# Local seed (guardrail: order-independent of any later relocation/reordering of
# other sections relative to this one -- see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md).
set.seed(8001)
alpha_fit_only <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = 0)
alpha    <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = slope_structural_sd)
alpha_mu <- mean(alpha)
alpha_se <- sd(alpha)
summary(alpha)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 -4.166  -3.089  -2.919  -2.920  -2.750  -1.993

The resulting differential slope distribution has mean -2.92 and SD 0.251. Fit-only draws are retained as alpha_fit_only so the Hoffman structural-uncertainty sensitivity can report before/after effects without changing the fitted C-PSD itself.

5. Step 2 — Rescale measured concentrations to a common size range

5.1 Power-law integration for rescaling factors

If the differential PSD follows dN/dL = k·L^a, the concentration in [L₁, L₂] is proportional to k/(a+1)·(L₂^(a+1) − L₁^(a+1)) (a ≠ −1). The rescaling correction factor is:

CF = N(L_target_min, L_target_max) / N(L_meas_min, L_meas_max)

correction_factor() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R (Coffin et al. 2022). The measured size range is bias-corrected using the C-PSD LOD window from cpsd_fit_all.

5.1.0 Convention guard: Koelmans et al. (2020) worked example

Because the correction-factor convention now drives both the exposure rescaling and (after SPEC 1b, below) the hazard-side ERM alignment, it is guarded here by a visible, rendered worked-example assertion rather than relying only on an unrendered test file. Koelmans et al. (2020) report that rescaling a measured 30–2000 µm range to a 1–5000 µm target range at a differential slope of α = 1.6 gives CF = 8.32 (e.g., 100 particles/L → 832 particles/L). The Koelmans α is expressed as a positive-magnitude differential (PDF) slope, so it is passed to correction_factor() as a = -1.6 with slope_convention = "differential". This guard enforces the differential convention used throughout the report; if the convention regresses (e.g., a cumulative slope is passed where a differential slope is expected), the assertion below fails loudly and the render stops.

Show the code 
cf_check <- correction_factor(
  a = -1.6, L_meas_min = 30, L_meas_max = 2000,
  L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, slope_convention = "differential"
)
stopifnot(abs(cf_check - 8.32) < 0.05)   # Koelmans et al. (2020) worked example

# Companion guard: lock the C-PSD cumulative-to-differential relationship
# (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) on a real fit object used throughout this report.
stopifnot(abs((cpsd_fit_all$a_psd) - (cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd - 1)) < 1e-6)

cat(sprintf(
  "Convention check passed: CF(30-2000 um -> 1-5000 um, alpha=1.6) = %.3f (Koelmans et al. 2020 reference: 8.32)\n",
  cf_check
))
Convention check passed: CF(30-2000 um -> 1-5000 um, alpha=1.6) = 8.319 (Koelmans et al. 2020 reference: 8.32)

The equivalent check is also encoded as an automated testthat guard in tests/testthat/test-correction_factor.R, so the convention is protected both in interactive/rendered use and in CI-style test runs.

Show the code 
# correct_and_bootstrap_eed() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles the LOD bias
# correction, the power-law correction_factor() rescale, the Monte Carlo corrected-
# concentration draws, and the EED bootstrap into one shared step used identically
# across river/sediment/ocean.
set.seed(9101)
river_corr <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
  monitoring  = monitoring,
  conc_col    = "C_measured_pL",
  cpsd_fit    = cpsd_fit_all,
  alpha_draws = alpha,
  L_tar_min   = 1,
  L_tar_max   = 5000,
  n_draws     = 3000,
  n_boot      = n_boot,
  probs       = c(0.5, 0.95),
  slope_convention = "differential"
)
monitoring         <- river_corr$monitoring
L_meas_min_use     <- river_corr$L_meas_min_use
L_meas_max_use     <- river_corr$L_meas_max_use
combined_cf        <- river_corr$combined_cf
C_corrected_draws  <- river_corr$C_corrected_draws
C_sample_median    <- river_corr$C_sample_median
eed_boot           <- river_corr$eed_boot

quantile(combined_cf, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
        5%        50%        95% 
  3106.256  22465.194 175514.080

The differential-slope convention (length, area, volume, mass) is the current basis; Appendix A quantifies the effect of each prior convention error.

The median rescaling factor is 22465.19 (90% CI: 3106.26 – 175514.08), applied to convert concentrations measured over 165 – 385 µm to the target range of 1 – 5000 µm. This is a model-based count correction: correction_factor() integrates the differential PSD exponent directly as L^(a + 1), and no internal conversion is applied when slope_convention = "differential".

5.2 Optional additional bias terms as probability distributions

Coffin et al. (2022) describe two additional multiplicative correction terms that can be composed with the power-law rescaling CF:

  • Fiber correction factor (\(\text{CF}_\text{fiber}\)): Accounts for systematic fiber under-retention during mesh-based sampling (net trawls, pump filtration with woven sieves). In those contexts, the slender geometry of fibers allows them to pass through mesh apertures lengthwise, producing under-counts that are proportional to mesh size (Zhao et al. 2026). A log-normal distribution is appropriate because the factor is right-skewed and strictly positive.
  • Plastic proportion factor (\(p_\text{plastic}\)): The fraction of detected particles confirmed as plastic by spectroscopy. A Beta(\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) distribution is appropriate because the factor is bounded to [0, 1].

Assessment for this dataset. A fiber correction factor is not applied here for two reasons:

  1. Sampling method: The present monitoring data are from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered whole-water grab samples (pump collection), not mesh net trawls. Zhao et al. (2026) demonstrate that the dramatic fiber under-capture they quantify (0.7% efficiency at 330 µm mesh) arises specifically from the geometric interaction of elongated particles with woven mesh apertures. Membrane pore filtration retains particles primarily by size, so this mechanism does not apply.
  2. Power-law extrapolation already corrects for sub-LOD fibers: The correction_factor() function in Step 2 uses the fitted power-law slope to integrate particle counts from the measured size range (50–500 µm) to the target range (1–5000 µm). This extrapolation already accounts for undetected small fibers in a self-consistent way. Applying an additional fiber CF on top would double-count this adjustment.

The fiber slope (\(a_\text{psd}\) = -2.67) is shallower than the fragment slope (-3.74), which may reflect residual under-retention of the finest fibers through nominal 50 µm filter pores, but this cannot be corrected without fiber-specific filter efficiency data. See Section 4.2.1.2 for the literature comparison.

Show the code 
# combined_cf was already computed above (Section 5.1, via correct_and_bootstrap_eed());
# the optional fiber/plastic-proportion factors described above are not multiplied in
# (neither is applicable to this µFTIR membrane-filter dataset -- see rationale above).
quantile(combined_cf, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
        5%        50%        95% 
  3106.256  22465.194 175514.080

5.3 Apply probabilistic correction to monitoring data

We treat each monitoring sample’s corrected concentration as:

C_corrected = C_measured * combined_cf_draw, with combined_cf_draw sampled in Monte Carlo.

This yields a distribution per monitoring sample, and a pooled exposure distribution across samples.

Show the code 
# For simplicity, assume the same CF distribution applies to each sample.
# If CF depends on site/method/shape, build CF distributions per strata and apply accordingly.
# C_corrected_draws was already computed above (Section 5.1, via correct_and_bootstrap_eed()).

C_corrected_draws |>
  summarise(p05 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.05),
            p50 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.50),
            p95 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.95))

1  37.9  706. 24661.

6. Step 3 — Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) via empirical bootstrap

Because environmental monitoring data are typically sparse and highly skewed, a nonparametric bootstrap is often a strong default:

  • Resample (with replacement) the corrected sample-level concentrations.
  • Compute the empirical CDF and desired percentiles per bootstrap replicate.
  • This avoids heavy reliance on a parametric distribution family selection for EEDs.
Show the code 
# Collapse each sample to its median corrected concentration, then bootstrap across samples.
# This isolates site-level variability from correction-factor uncertainty (handled in MC2D below).

# correct_and_bootstrap_eed(), which internally calls bootstrap_eed()).

7.2 Hazard-side particle-trait parameter matrix

SPEC 1b correction (differential vs. cumulative volume/area slope). The particle-trait alignment parameters a.v.* (volume) and a.sa.* (surface area) in PSSDplusplus::param_default_values use the same differential ERM-slope convention as the length parameter alpha.* — consistent with the Kooi et al. (2021) mean-ERM formula and the Koelmans et al. (2020)/Coffin et al. (2022) rescaling equation (Section 5.1). A prior version of this analysis passed the cumulative C-PSD slope ($a_cpsd) into a.v.*/a.sa.* instead of the differential slope ($a_psd = a_cpsd - 1), leaving these parameters exactly 1.0 too shallow. Because the pSSD++ Food Dilution model computes a volumetric dose from the polydisperse mean particle volume, and the mean of a power-law distribution is acutely sensitive to how far the exponent is above or below 1, this ~1.0 shortfall in a.v inflated the mean particle volume — and therefore the Food Dilution risk quotient — by several orders of magnitude relative to the corrected value. a.m.* (mass) is set consistently with a.v.* below, since mass is proportional to volume at constant density; the two are asserted to agree within 0.3 as an internal consistency check. This correction is confined to the hazard-side alignment parameters; the exposure-side correction_factor() count rescaling (Section 5.1) already used the length-based differential slope only and is unaffected.

Show the code 
# replace the default parameter matrix distribution with values derived using the C-PSD method here
param_values <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values |>
  # update parameters from C-PSD method
  mutate(alpha.freshwater = -alpha_mu, # positive magnitude of differential a_psd where dN/dL = k * L^a
         alpha.freshwater.sd = alpha_se,
         # additional values need updating:
         ### Length to width ratio
         R.ave.water.freshwater = R.ave_mean,
         R.ave.water.freshwater.sd = R.ave_sd,

         ### polymer density
         #p.ave.freshwater = ,
         #p.ave.freshwater.sd = ,

         ### volume (SPEC 1b: differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd;
         ### the cumulative slope is exactly 1.0 too shallow and inflates the
         ### polydisperse mean particle volume, deflating the Food Dilution threshold)
         a.v.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_volume$a_psd,
         a.v.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_psd,

         ### mass (mass ~ density * volume; at constant density this shares volume's
         ### differential slope, so set from data for consistency with a.v rather than
         ### retaining the unrelated package default, which would leave a.v/a.m mismatched)
         a.m.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_volume$a_psd,
         a.m.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_psd,

         ### surface area
         a.sa.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_area$a_psd,# derived value for all shapes
         a.sa.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_area$se_a_psd
         )

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent (mass ~ volume
# at constant density); flag rather than silently pass if they diverge materially.
stopifnot(abs(param_values$a.v.freshwater - param_values$a.m.freshwater) < 0.3)

# generate parameter matrix using bespoke environmental parameter values
set.seed(7001)
param_matrix <- matrix_function(
  n = n_boot, #size of matrix (10,000 is recommended)
  params = param_values, #parameter distribution values 
  #params = PSSDplusplus::param_default_values, #beta-test with defaults
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500, # maximum particle size (microns) to truncate tissue tranlocation size limit distribution to based on biological plausibility
  x1M_set = 1, #minimum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
  x2D_set = 5000 #maximum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
) |> 
  # replace R.ave.water.freshwater with bootstrapped values
   mutate(R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
          H_W_ratio.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE)) #H_W ratio is assumed same as length-width ratio

# visualize parameter distributions
param_plots <- parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix) # generate parameter distribution plots
#visualize plots
alpha_combined_plot_river <- param_plots$alpha_combined_plot # distribution of alpha parameters
alpha_combined_plot_river <- label_matrix(alpha_combined_plot_river, "River water")

ggsave(alpha_combined_plot_river, filename = "figures/alpha_combined_plot_river.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
alpha_combined_plot_river

7.3 Run Monte-Carlo Simulation on Toxicity Data using Parameter Matrix

MC_sim_align_parallel() is the core PSSDplusplus function that aligns each toxicological endpoint to the particle trait distributions defined in param_matrix. For each Monte Carlo replicate (\(i = 1, \ldots, n_\text{sim}\)) it:

  1. Draws a particle trait vector from param_matrix: particle size (\(L\), log-normal), aspect ratio (\(AR\)), density (\(\rho\)), and C-PSD slope (\(\alpha_\text{cpsd}\)).
  2. Applies the bioaccessibility model for each ERM:
    • Food Dilution — computes the volumetric food dilution dose (particles/L) using the particle volume and the organism’s gut volume, converting the reported NOEC/EC dose to an environmentally comparable particle concentration.
    • Tissue Translocation — computes the particle flux to tissue using the size-dependent translocation model; only particles below the translocation size threshold (500 µm) are included.
  3. Aligns each species’ EC dose to a common concentration unit (particles/L equivalent), enabling a multi-species SSD to be constructed from studies that used different MP sizes, shapes, and concentrations.

The output MC_sim_df is a long data frame with one row per toxicological endpoint per Monte Carlo replicate, with columns for the aligned dose (particles_L_food_dilution, particles_L_ox_stress), bioaccessibility group (ingestible, translocatable), and quality tier (risk.13, bio_f). It is then split by ERM and filtered to the relevant endpoints before SSD fitting in Section 7.4.

Show the code 
# run_pssd_pipeline() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles MC_sim_align_parallel(),
# the ERM-specific results_df filtering, erm_registry construction, and make_all_pSSDs()
# into one step used identically across river/sediment/ocean.
river_pssd <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data,
  param_matrix = param_matrix,
  environments = c("Freshwater"),
  cache_suffix = "river",
  dose_unit    = "L",
  n_sim        = n_boot,
  num_cores    = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",
  seed         = 5001
)
MC_sim_df    <- river_pssd$MC_sim_df
erm_registry <- river_pssd$erm_registry

The output MC_sim_df is a long data frame with one row per toxicological endpoint per Monte Carlo replicate, with columns for the aligned dose (particles_L_food_dilution, particles_L_ox_stress), bioaccessibility group (ingestible, translocatable), and quality tier (risk.13, bio_f). It is split by ERM into erm_registry (Food Dilution / Tissue Translocation subsets) before SSD fitting below.

8. Step 5 — Risk characterization using joint distributions (Monte Carlo)

We now combine: - Exposure: bootstrap distribution (e.g., EED 50th percentile) or full empirical sample distribution. - Hazard: pSSD++-derived HC5/HC10 distributions for each ERM.

A common probabilistic risk metric is: - Risk Quotient (RQ): RQ = Exposure / Hazard. - Probability of exceedance: P(RQ > 1).

Below we compute four RQ distributions: [Food dilution, Tissue translocation] x [HC5, HC10].

Show the code 
# draw_rq_mc1d() and summarize_rq() are sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
n_risk     <- 1000

9. Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D)

Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D) to separately handle: - uncertainty (e.g., correction factors, hazard model uncertainty), - variability (true spatial/temporal variability in exposure).

Below, the outer loop samples uncertain parameters (a correction factor draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx), while the inner loop samples exposure variability from the observed monitoring concentrations.

How to read the MC2D outputs

  • Each outer iteration represents one plausible “world” of uncertainty (sampling one CF draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx).
  • Within that world, the inner loop samples exposure variability across sites/dates (using the observed measured concentrations).
  • For each outer iteration, we summarize the resulting RQ distribution as P_exceed, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, and RQ_p99.
  • The distribution of these summaries across iterations quantifies uncertainty in risk metrics, while the inner loop represents variability in exposure.
Show the code 
# mc2d_risk() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
# Outer loop: n_uncertainty = 300 CF + hazard draws (uncertainty).
# Inner loop: n_variability = 1000 exposure draws per outer iteration (variability).
mc2d_results <- mc2d_risk(
  monitoring_df = monitoring,
  combined_cf   = combined_cf,
  haz_df        = haz,
  n_uncertainty = 300,
  n_variability = 1000,
  seed          = 1
)

mc2d_summary <- mc2d_results |>
  dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
  summarise(
    P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
    P_exceed_p95 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.95),
    P_exceed_p05 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.05),
    RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
    RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

10. Sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analysis to identify dominant uncertainty contributors (e.g., alpha, plastic proportion, analytical recovery).

10.0 Hoffman et al. (2026) transport and slope-structure diagnostics

Hoffman et al. (2026) show that vertical transport can make a sampled PSD deviate from a single power law, with apparent slopes differing from the underlying PSD by about two exponent units across a critical size. The following diagnostics are model-based sensitivities. They do not replace the production CF, but they show how much the Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation risk summaries move when the slope uncertainty is widened beyond OLS fit error and when surface/subsurface samples are analyzed separately.

Show the code 
summarize_mc2d_hc5 <- function(x) {
  x |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
      RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
      RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

slope_sd_grid <- c(0, slope_structural_sd, 0.5, 1.0)
hoffman_slope_sensitivity <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(slope_sd_grid, function(sd_i) {
  set.seed(1000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000))
  alpha_i <- alpha_dist(
    mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd,
    sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd,
    n = 3000,
    structural_sd = sd_i
  )
  cf_i <- correction_factor(
    a = alpha_i,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min_use,
    L_meas_max = L_meas_max_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  mc_i <- mc2d_risk(
    monitoring_df = monitoring,
    combined_cf = cf_i,
    haz_df = haz,
    n_uncertainty = 100,
    n_variability = 500,
    seed = 2000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000)
  )
  summarize_mc2d_hc5(mc_i) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      structural_sd = sd_i,
      CF_p50 = median(cf_i),
      CF_p95 = quantile(cf_i, 0.95)
    )
}))

10.0.1 By-river risk characterization (not pooled)

The headline river assessment pools particle and monitoring data across all four sampling locations (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San Lorenzo) into a single C-PSD fit and a single exposure distribution. This section instead runs the full workflow – C-PSD fit, differential-slope draws, correction factor, EED bootstrap, and Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation risk characterization – independently for each river, reusing each location’s C-PSD fit already computed in Section 4.2.1 (cpsd_fits_by_loc) and each river’s own monitoring replicates, but the same production hazard distribution (haz) throughout, since species toxicity does not depend on which river was sampled. This tests whether the pooled result masks location-specific differences in exposure (driven by each river’s own particle-size slope and measured concentrations) rather than assuming one river is representative of all four.

Show the code 
river_hc5_risk <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(locations, function(loc) {
  fit_i     <- cpsd_fits_by_loc[[loc]]
  seed_base <- 41000 + match(loc, locations) * 10

  set.seed(seed_base)
  alpha_i <- alpha_dist(mu = fit_i$a_psd, sd = fit_i$se_a_psd, n = 3000, structural_sd = slope_structural_sd)

  mon_i <- monitoring |> dplyr::filter(river == loc)

  set.seed(seed_base + 1)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = mon_i, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = fit_i, alpha_draws = alpha_i,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot,
    probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
  )

  set.seed(seed_base + 2)
  risk_draws_i <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz, corr_i$eed_boot$q50, n_risk = 1000) |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5)

  risk_draws_i |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      RQ_p5    = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p50   = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p95   = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
      P_exceed = mean(RQ > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      river        = loc,
      n_monitoring = nrow(mon_i),
      n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_river$sample_location == loc),
      a_psd        = fit_i$a_psd,
      CF_p50       = stats::median(corr_i$combined_cf)
    )
}))

10.1 Morris global sensitivity analysis (future work)

A Morris elementary-effects screen (global sensitivity ranking of RQ uncertainty drivers) is deferred to a dedicated compute pass: it repeatedly rebuilds small pSSD++ hazard models and, at a budget large enough to produce a stable ranking, is too slow for a routine report render. It did not run in this render.

10.2 µFTIR objective: critical assessment of the detection floor and its intersection with the LOD/CF workflow

Instrument configuration

The µFTIR analysis used an objective equivalent to ~4× magnification with 25 µm pixel size. At this pixel resolution, the practical minimum detectable particle size (requiring ≥ 2 pixels across the shortest dimension) is approximately 50 µm — consistent with the L_meas_min = 50 µm parameter used throughout this workflow. This value is already embedded in the correction factor (CF) calculation and is not an additional bias to correct.

Why the Wang et al. (2026) ×33 scaling factor does not apply here

Wang et al. (2026) found that a 4× µFTIR objective (20 µm pixel) detects only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to a 25× reference (2 µm pixel). At face value this suggests a ×33 upward scaling should be applied to our concentrations. This is incorrect for the following reasons:

1. The 97% “missed” particles lie almost entirely below our measurement floor.

The 25× objective in Wang et al. detects particles as small as ~4 µm. The 4× objective detects only those ≥ ~40–50 µm. The difference (97% of total particle count) is dominated by particles in the 4–50 µm size class. Our workflow already treats L_meas_min = 50 µm as the lower detection floor and uses the power-law CF to extrapolate particle counts from this floor down to 1 µm. The Wang et al. sub-50 µm particles are not “missing” from our analysis — they are the precise population that the correction_factor() function reconstructs via power-law integration.

2. Within the measured range (50–500 µm), the 4×/25 µm system is effective.

At 25 µm pixel size:

Particle size Pixels across Detection status
50 µm 2 px Marginal (meets minimum)
100 µm 4 px Reliable
200 µm 8 px Well-resolved
500 µm 20 px Fully resolved

For particles at or above 100 µm — which covers the entire Segur LOD fitting window (fragments: 95–350 µm; all shapes: 165–385 µm) — detection is reliable with this pixel size. The ×33 correction factor was derived from total particle counts including the sub-50 µm population; it does not represent within-range inefficiency.

3. The Segur LOD algorithm implicitly handles the marginal 50–100 µm zone.

The Segur LOD search specifically identifies the size window where the C-PSD is most linear (\(R^2 \geq 0.90\)). The 50–100 µm region, where detection by the 4×/25 µm system may be incomplete, would manifest as a deviation from power-law behavior at the lower end of the binned distribution — and would therefore be excluded from the fitting window. Indeed, the fitted lower LODs (95 µm for fragments, 165 µm pooled) are well above 50 µm, confirming that the algorithm already pushed the lower bound into the reliable detection zone.

4. Applying ×33 on top of the existing CF would double-count.

The current CF has a median of 22465.2× (90% CI: 3106.3–175514.1×). This already accounts for the unmeasured sub-50 µm population via power-law extrapolation. Multiplying C_corrected by an additional 33× would apply a second, conflicting correction to the same particle pool, producing a total inflation factor of ~741351× — far in excess of any defensible estimate.

Residual uncertainty: the 50–100 µm marginal zone

The one genuine uncertainty from the 4×/25 µm configuration is incomplete counting in the 50–100 µm particle size class. Particles in this range occupy 2–4 pixels and may be undercounted by approximately 10–30% relative to what a 15× system would detect. The sensitivity analysis below quantifies the effect of adjusting L_meas_min from 50 µm to 100 µm, which effectively removes the marginal zone from the measured concentration estimate and lets the CF extrapolate it instead.

Show the code 
# Compare CF and risk outcomes under two L_meas_min assumptions:
# 50 µm (current, includes marginal zone) vs 100 µm (excludes marginal zone — conservative floor)
lmeas_scenarios <- list(
  "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)" = list(L_lo = 50,  L_hi = 500),
  "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)" = list(L_lo = 100, L_hi = 500)
)

lmeas_cf_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(lmeas_scenarios), function(scen) {
  s   <- lmeas_scenarios[[scen]]
  cf_s <- correction_factor(
    a           = alpha,                  # differential a_psd draws (n_mc)
    L_meas_min  = s$L_lo,
    L_meas_max  = s$L_hi,
    L_tar_min   = 1,
    L_tar_max   = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  data.frame(
    scenario = scen,
    CF_p05   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.05),  1),
    CF_med   = round(median(cf_s),           1),
    CF_p95   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.95),  1)
  )
}))

    "n_mc = ", n_mc, " Monte Carlo draws."
  ),

)

5%…1 L_meas_min = 50 µm (current) 381.0 1846.7 9344.6
5%…2 L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative) 1153.7 7231.1 48078.7

Raising L_meas_min from 50 to 100 µm increases the median CF from 1846.7× to 7231.1× — a modest change that reflects the additional particles in the 50–100 µm range being moved from “measured” to “extrapolated.” This is the appropriate sensitivity analysis for this instrument configuration: it brackets the range of outcomes depending on whether the marginal detection zone is treated as reliably measured or excluded and reconstructed via power-law. The current workflow (L_meas_min = 50 µm) is the less conservative (lower CF) choice; if the 50–100 µm counts are systematically low due to detection limits, the true concentration may be closer to the L_meas_min = 100 µm estimate.

Summary. No additional objective-based correction factor is applied to C_measured_pL. The existing workflow already accounts for instrument detection limits through (1) the L_meas_min = 50 µm floor that reflects the 4×/25 µm pixel detection limit, and (2) the power-law CF that extrapolates particle counts from this floor to the 1 µm target. The Segur LOD fitting window (≥ 165 µm) lies entirely within the reliable detection zone of the instrument. The Wang et al. (2026) ×33 factor would be appropriate only if converting a 4× total particle count to an equivalent 25× total count without any power-law extrapolation — not in combination with the CF approach used here.

11. Sediment — Beach Sand

11.1 Derive power-law values from raw sediment particle data

Show the code 
# import sediment particle data (beach sand as sediment proxy)
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles |> 
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand") |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl)

# ---- Thickness (height) factor from sediment data ----
ratio_tbl_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1 / aspect_ratio,
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ---- Volumes ----
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl_sed |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

11.3.0 Sediment concentration provenance audit

Before treating any sediment concentration as a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value, this subsection verifies where it actually comes from. The check below is rendered so the finding is auditable rather than asserted.

Show the code

(a single fixed value here -- independent of which sediment sample/date/location -- is the signature of a per-liter processing/pumped-volume normalization, not a per-kg dry-sediment-mass normalization, since no two real sediment samples share an identical dry mass)
Show the code 
has_mass_or_density_col <- any(grepl("mass|weight|density|dry|bulk", names(part_dets_summ_raw), ignore.case = TRUE))
cat("\nAny sample dry-weight / wet-weight / bulk-density column present in the source data:",
    has_mass_or_density_col, "\n")

Any sample dry-weight / wet-weight / bulk-density column present in the source data: FALSE

Finding (SPEC 1d-i). extrap_conc_PPL — the only concentration column in data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds — is constructed identically for every sample_type (river water, ocean water, and beach sand/sediment): extrap_count divided by a single fixed volume-like denominator, with no sediment sample dry-mass, wet-mass, or bulk-density column present anywhere in the source data to convert it to particles/kg dry weight. Concretely, monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg was set to this same per-liter-type column (extrap_conc_PPL) with a # placeholder comment, i.e., a per-liter water/processing-volume value was carried through the sediment pipeline and reported as if it were particles/kg sediment. No genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment concentration exists in the data available to this analysis (verified above; Opt_micro_all_cut.rds, a separate large-microplastics dataset, similarly records beach-sand samples on a Volume_Pumped_L basis, not a dry-sediment-mass basis). Per SPEC 1d-i, the sediment concentration pathway is therefore flagged non-quantitative/illustrative rather than corrected in place (there is nothing to convert it to), and is excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) – see the flag and downstream caveats below.

Show the code 
# set to TRUE only once a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment
# concentration (from a real sediment sample mass) is available; the sediment
# EED/RQ machinery below is retained for illustrative/methods purposes (e.g. to
# confirm the slope-convention fix direction in Section 13.1) but must not be
# read as a real risk estimate while this flag is FALSE.
sediment_concentration_is_quantitative <- FALSE

    sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate,
    # SPEC 1d-i: NOT a genuine particles/kg sediment concentration -- this is the

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater - param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater) < 0.3)

# SPEC 1d-iv (rule-out): confirm the sediment alignment slopes are on the
# differential convention -- i.e. this analysis' large sediment RQ is NOT
# attributable to a slope-convention error (that was SPEC 1b, already fixed
# and asserted above). a.v/a.sa/a.m are exact deterministic transforms of
# their fits (-a_psd), so those are checked tightly. alpha.sediment.freshwater
# is instead the MEAN of a Monte Carlo truncated-normal sample centered on
# a_psd (alpha_dist(), which also widens SD by slope_structural_sd) -- it is
# expected to be close to, but not bit-identical to, -(a_cpsd - 1), so it is
# checked with a tolerance appropriate for MC sampling noise rather than an
# exact-equality tolerance.
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater - (-(cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd - 1))) < 0.2)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater  - (-(cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
cat(sprintf(
  "SPEC 1d-iv rule-out PASSED: sediment slopes are on the differential convention (alpha=%.3f, a.v=%.3f, a.sa=%.3f, a.m=%.3f). The sediment RQ magnitude is therefore driven by the concentration/unit issues in Section 11.3.0/11.4 (SPEC 1d-i/ii), not by the slope convention.\n",
  param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater,
  param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater
))
SPEC 1d-iv rule-out PASSED: sediment slopes are on the differential convention (alpha=2.984, a.v=1.705, a.sa=2.207, a.m=1.705). The sediment RQ magnitude is therefore driven by the concentration/unit issues in Section 11.3.0/11.4 (SPEC 1d-i/ii), not by the slope convention.

SPEC 1d-iv finding. The sediment alignment slopes above are already on the correct differential convention (asserted, not merely observed) and are mutually consistent (a.v ≈ a.m). The implausibly large sediment Food Dilution RQ documented in Section 11.4/15 is therefore not caused by a slope-convention error — that class of error was SPEC 1b’s fix and is independently guarded here — but by the exposure-concentration provenance issue documented in Section 11.3.0 (SPEC 1d-i) and/or the hazard-unit-scale question examined in Section 11.4 (SPEC 1d-ii).

11.4 Sediment probabilistic risk characterization

11.4.0 hazard-side unit-alignment trace

Before reading the sediment RQ below, this subsection traces whether dose_unit = "kg" genuinely carries particles/kg-dry-weight units end-to-end on the hazard side, independent of the exposure-side problem documented in Section 11.3.0.

Show the code 
# Inspect the raw ToMEx sediment-exposure dose columns feeding tox_data_sed,
# and confirm PSSDplusplus's dose_unit = "kg" pathway sources them directly
# (source inspection of PSSDplusplus::align_data()/convert_units_fxn() during

Finding (SPEC 1d-ii). The raw sediment-exposure toxicity doses in ToMEx (dose.particles.kg.sediment.master) span a physically plausible particles/kg-dry-weight range (tens to ~10^10), consistent with the order of magnitude of Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023)’s benthic HC5 (4.9×10⁹ particles/kg dw). No hardcoded water-to-sediment unit-conversion factor (e.g., a missing bulk-density or dry-weight scalar) was found in the dose_unit = "kg" code path: run_pssd_pipeline(..., dose_unit = "kg") (R/mp_risk_utils.R) selects the particles_kg_food_dilution/particles_kg_ox_stress columns from PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()’s output, which in turn are populated directly from each sediment study’s own reported particles/kg dose (via align_data()’s dose.particles.kg.master coalescing chain), not derived from a water-based value. The hazard side therefore appears to be genuinely unit-consistent on its own terms. The implausibly low derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 (exact value in the guard below) cannot be attributed to a discrete missing-conversion bug found in this trace; it is more likely size-alignment sensitivity to the sediment ERM exponents (the same mechanism SPEC 1b addressed for Food Dilution) for whichever study anchors the low tail, amplified by SSD-extrapolation noise on a modest sediment toxicity dataset (89 records). This remains an open question rather than a resolved code fix, since (unlike SPEC 1d-i) no single incorrect line was identified. Regardless, because the exposure-side concentration is already known to be non-quantitative, this hazard-side question does not change the conclusion that the sediment RQ/HC5 below must be excluded from the headline risk characterization.

  cat(sprintf(

  ))

SPEC 1d-iii benthic-HC5 sanity guard: Food Dilution HC5 FAILS the plausible benthic range (1e1-1e12 particles/kg dw); Tissue Translocation HC5 PASSES it. `sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` is FALSE (SPEC 1d-i), so this guard is intentionally rendered as a non-fatal loud message rather than a hard stopifnot() -- it becomes a hard, render-halting assertion the instant that flag is set TRUE. A FAIL here is EXPECTED and is additional confirmation that the current sediment pathway must not be reported as a real risk finding.

The current derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails the plausibility guard above by roughly eleven orders of magnitude (see the rendered value; expected to be on the order of 0.0928 particles/kg vs. a published benthic range of 10¹-10¹² particles/kg dw), consistent with the SPEC 1d-i finding that the sediment pathway’s exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. The sediment Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation RQ/HC5 figures in this report are illustrative/non-quantitative and are excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) pending a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration.

11.5 Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment

Rationale. Sediment is an accumulating, long-residence depositional compartment, and it is the sink for the large/dense particles that differential settling removes from the water column (Hoffman et al. 2026; the critical-size capture-fraction diagnostic in Section 13 quantifies that filtering mechanism for this dataset). Those deposited particles continue to fragment in situ, so — per Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — both exposure (bioaccessible particle number) and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species are size-accessible) are dynamic rather than static. A single-time-point sediment RQ is therefore a snapshot that can under-represent future risk in an accumulating bed. Everything in this section is a framework upgrade, not a live risk calculation: the sediment exposure concentration remains non-quantitative (sediment_concentration_is_quantitative = FALSE, SPEC 1d), so nothing here re-introduces sediment into the headline risk conclusion (Sections 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3).

11.5.1 Temporal fragmentation framing

  • Sediment is treated as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment. Deposited microplastics continue to fragment, shifting the particle-size distribution toward smaller, more numerous, more bioaccessible particles over residence time in the bed.
  • Consequently, any static sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot. Both HC5 (which benthic species are size-accessible) and bioaccessible exposure evolve as fragmentation proceeds — the single-time-point Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation figures in Section 11.4 describe the sediment PSD’s condition at the time of sampling, not its trajectory.
  • This compounds, rather than substitutes for, the SPEC 1d exposure-concentration problem. Even once a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration becomes available, a single power-law fit to that concentration would still understate risk relative to the bed’s future, more-fragmented state.
  • Cite Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — a prospective, temporally-explicit risk framework for fragmenting microplastics (size-independent fragmentation rate constant kfrag, doubling time TD) in which HC5 and RCR are time-dependent because shrinking particles become bioaccessible to progressively more sensitive species; the source paper’s median HC5 example drops from 2.1×10⁴ to 1.95×10³ particles/kg when a sensitive species becomes accessible, and individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community SSD by roughly a decade. Cross-reference: the Hoffman et al. (2026) differential-settling sink argument already used in this document (Section 13’s critical-size diagnostic) is the mechanism that puts large/dense particles into the sediment bed in the first place; SPEC 1e is about what happens to them after they arrive.

11.5.3 Time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

Making the existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility size-gate explicitly time-dependent (HC5(t)/RCR(t) as a trajectory) is deferred: it needs a residence-time/age-of-deposition axis that does not exist in the source sediment dataset. Full scoping in Appendix C.

11.5.4 Most-sensitive-species screen (sediment)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal by roughly a decade, and the sediment benthic SSD here is small and comparatively unstable (89 records, 9 species). This screen identifies the single most sensitive species (lowest aligned effect dose) per ERM and reports it alongside the community HC5 already computed in Section 11.4 — as an early-warning companion, not a replacement.

For Food Dilution, the single most sensitive species among the 7 sediment benthic species considered is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 1.42 particles/kg dw, 300 aligned records), compared with the community Food Dilution HC5 of 0.0928 particles/kg dw computed in Section 11.4. For Tissue Translocation, the most sensitive species is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 167 particles/kg dw, 300 records), compared with the community Tissue Translocation HC5 of 12.2 particles/kg dw. As Section 11.5.3 notes, a finer PSD from continued fragmentation could bring additional, potentially more sensitive species into bioaccessible range over time, which is part of why this individual-species screen is worth tracking alongside the community HC5 rather than assuming the current community SSD is stable. This screen does not change the sediment exclusion from the headline conclusion (its inputs are the same non-quantitative-exposure sediment pathway); the companion individual-species screen for the quantitative river/ocean water compartments is reported in Section 15.4, once every matrix’s hazard objects have been computed.

12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

Particle volume computation

Show the code 
# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
    "| shapes:", paste(sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$shape)), collapse = ", "), "\n")

Particle volume

Note: ocean’s fragment volume fit uses the same length/width-consistent volume_lod_bounds() approach as river and sediment (Section 4.2.3). Its fiber fit does not: ocean has only 11 fiber particles total, and even the corrected (length/width-consistent, not isotropic) fiber volume-LOD window contains just 4 of them — too few to constrain a fit. Ocean’s fiber volume fit instead falls back to the Segur algorithm’s own auto-detected LOD window. Similarly, the “all” (pooled shapes) fit uses the fragment-only volume-LOD window rather than the fragment/fiber union: with only 11 fibers, the union window is dominated by a handful of sparse, noisy fiber-derived bounds and destabilizes the pooled fit (fragments outnumber fibers roughly 10:1 in this matrix, so anchoring “all” to fragment’s reliable range is the more defensible choice here).

Show the code

r_med_fiber_ocean <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fiber"]

# fragment and all use the same uniform vol_bin_um as river/sediment. fiber is the one
# documented exception (see note above): with only 4 particles inside its physically-
# derived window, no fixed window is viable, so it falls back to auto-detection
# (fit_range_um = NA) with a coarser bin width appropriate to its much wider absolute
# volume range (up to ~3e7 µm³, vs ~7e5 µm³ for fragment) — fine bins there would be
# almost entirely empty regardless of methodology, per the small-sample diagnosis above.
ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um <- 1e6
cpsd_fits_ocean_volume <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "V_um3",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment)
  )
)
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fragment
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fiber
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$all

Parameter distributions

Show the code 
set.seed(9003)
R.ave_ocean_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_ocean$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_ocean_vals   <- R.ave_ocean_result$vals
R.ave_ocean_mean   <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_mean
R.ave_ocean_sd     <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_sd

param_values_ocean <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine"]]          <- -alpha_ocean_mu
param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine.sd"]]       <- alpha_ocean_se
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine"]]    <- R.ave_ocean_mean
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine.sd"]] <- R.ave_ocean_sd
# use the differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd
# (the cumulative value is 1.0 too shallow; see river/sediment blocks above).
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine"]]           <- -cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine.sd"]]        <- cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_psd
# a.m.marine: use volume slope as proxy (mass ∝ density × volume; constant density → same slope)
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_psd
# Keep all remaining params from param_default_values (same pattern as river section)
# a.ssa.marine, p.ave.marine etc. retain their validated defaults

Build and visualize parameter distributions

Show the code 
set.seed(7003)
param_matrix_ocean <- matrix_function(
  n    = n_boot,
  params = param_values_ocean,
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
  x1M_set = 1,
  x2D_set = 5000,
  include_marine_surface_water     = TRUE,
  include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
  include_marine_sediment          = FALSE,
  include_freshwater_sediment      = FALSE
)

ocean_R_col  <- rlang::sym("R.ave.water.marine")
ocean_HW_col <- rlang::sym("H_W_ratio.water.marine")

param_matrix_ocean <- param_matrix_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    !!ocean_R_col  := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    !!ocean_HW_col := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )

tryCatch(
  {
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean <- parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix_ocean, compartments = c("Marine Surface Water"))$alpha_combined_plot
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean <- label_matrix(alpha_combined_plot_ocean, "Ocean water")
    ggsave(alpha_combined_plot_ocean, filename = "figures/alpha_combined_plot_ocean.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean
  },

Align toxicity data

Show the code 
# run_pssd_pipeline() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles MC_sim_align_parallel(),
# the ERM-specific results_df filtering, erm_registry construction, and make_all_pSSDs()
# into one step used identically across river/sediment/ocean.
ocean_pssd <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data_ocean,
  param_matrix = param_matrix_ocean,
  environments = c("Marine"),
  cache_suffix = "ocean",
  dose_unit    = "L",
  n_sim        = n_boot,
  num_cores    = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",
  seed         = 5003
)
MC_sim_df_ocean    <- ocean_pssd$MC_sim_df
erm_registry_ocean <- ocean_pssd$erm_registry

# 1D Monte Carlo risk quotient — added for parity with river/sediment (both already have
# this step); ocean previously had only the 2D MC2D characterization below.

Results at a glance

River and ocean water (the quantitative headline result). At HC5, river water Food Dilution median RQ = 7.88 (P(RQ>1) = 100%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0.194 (P(RQ>1) = 20.1%); ocean water Food Dilution median RQ = 3.28 (P(RQ>1) = 73.8%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0.037 (P(RQ>1) = 7.8%). Food Dilution is risk-dominant; Tissue Translocation is below threshold at the median, for both matrices. The single-slope exposure correction (used above) and a piecewise (dual-slope) bounding sensitivity bracket the sub-detection-limit extrapolation; both are quantified in the Sensitivity & structural uncertainty section below. Sediment is excluded from this conclusion: its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis, not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement, and its nominal Food Dilution RQ (153,011, P = 100%) fails a benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude (Section 11). A fully quantified executive summary, including the RQ decomposition that separates the exposure/length-slope/area-slope/volume-slope contributions, follows in Key Findings below.

Hoffman et al. (2026) frame the observed PSD as a transport-filtered distribution. A simple diagnostic is the capture fraction f(d, δ) = 1 − exp(−ws(d)·δ / K) and the critical size where ws(d)·δ / K ≈ 1. The calculation below uses Stokes settling/rise speed with user-supplied delta_m = 0.1 m and K_m2_s = 0.00001 m^2/s. These are assumptions, not measured site parameters, and should be replaced with field-specific values before a mechanistic transport correction is attempted.

Show the code 
matrix_fit_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Matrix = c("River water", "Sediment", "Ocean water"),
  cpsd_fit = list(cpsd_fit_all, cpsd_fit_sed_all, cpsd_fit_ocean_all),
  median_density_g_cm3 = c(
    median(raw_particles_river$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_sed$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_ocean$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  water_density_g_cm3 = c(1.00, 1.00, 1.025)
)

critical_piecewise_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(matrix_fit_tbl)), function(i) {
  fit_i <- matrix_fit_tbl$cpsd_fit[[i]]
  dc_i <- estimate_critical_size(
    delta_m = hoffman_delta_m,
    K_m2_s = hoffman_K_m2_s,
    density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    water_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$water_density_g_cm3[i]
  )
  pw_i <- piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic(fit_i)
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_fit_tbl$Matrix[i],
    median_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    critical_size_um = dc_i,
    fit_lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
    fit_lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    straddles_critical_size = is.finite(dc_i) && dc_i >= fit_i$lower_lod_used_um && dc_i <= fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    single_a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
    single_a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
    piecewise_break_um = pw_i$break_um,
    piecewise_low_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_low,
    piecewise_high_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_high,
    piecewise_delta_aic = pw_i$delta_aic
  )
}))
