The piecewise fits are diagnostic only. A fit window that straddles the assumed critical size is flagged because the fitted single slope may blend a transport-distorted fine-size regime with the coarser-size regime. Per Hoffman et al. (2026), future refinement should prioritize measured 3-D geometry and polymer density over increasingly elaborate settling equations; even precise-geometry settling models retain substantial residual error, so settling-based corrections should be treated as bias-level adjustments rather than high-precision concentration estimates.

13.3 Piecewise (dual-slope) PSD as a bounding exposure case

The production correction_factor() extrapolates a single fitted power-law slope from the measured LOD window down to the 1 um target floor. The two-segment diagnostic above (§13.2) shows the data themselves often prefer a shallower fine-size slope below a break point and a steeper coarse-size slope above it (river ΔAIC in the diagnostic table strongly favors the two-segment model; sediment likewise). Because the sub-floor extrapolation zone (1 um to the fitted LOD) can straddle or sit near that break — and because the fitted critical size d_c for river (~36 um) falls inside that 1-50 um extrapolation zone rather than inside the fit window itself — a single coarse slope may not be the right model to extrapolate through that zone. Independent evidence that single power laws mis-extrapolate to small, unmeasured sizes: in the St Louis Estuary, a single power law extrapolated to 1.3-12 particles/L for 5-5000 um while flow cytometry directly measured 600-1,600 particles/L in the same system (Thomas et al. 2024), and Segur et al. (2026) find size-aligned 1-5000 um concentrations average ~600x higher than reported values based on single-slope extrapolation. Both are cited as evidence that single-power-law extrapolation to small sizes is unreliable in general, not as a validated correction for this dataset.

correction_factor_piecewise() (R/mp_risk_utils.R, SPEC 2b) implements the two-segment alternative: it integrates dN/dL = kL^a using the fine-segment differential slope over [1, break_um] and the coarse-segment differential slope over [break_um, 5000], with the coarse segment’s density scaled so the two segments meet exactly (are continuous) at break_um. The piecewise cumulative slopes from the §13.2 diagnostic are converted to the differential convention (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) internally via slope_convention = "cumulative", consistent with the SPEC 1c guard. This is a labeled bounding sensitivity, not a replacement for the single-slope production CF — the production exposure pipeline (Sections 5-6, 9-10, 12) is unchanged. The 1 um-LOD_low sub-window is unconstrained by data in both* the single-slope and piecewise case; the piecewise result quantifies structural (model-form) uncertainty in how that unconstrained sub-window is extrapolated, which is not captured by the Gaussian slope_structural_sd already added to the fit-uncertainty propagation.

Show the code 
piecewise_cf_row <- function(matrix_label, piecewise_row, L_meas_min, L_meas_max) {
  brk <- piecewise_row$piecewise_break_um
  s_lo <- piecewise_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd
  s_hi <- piecewise_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd
  if (!is.finite(brk) || !is.finite(s_lo) || !is.finite(s_hi)) {
    return(tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = NA_real_, cf_piecewise = NA_real_))
  }
  cf_pw <- correction_factor_piecewise(
    a_low = s_lo, a_high = s_hi, break_um = brk,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "cumulative"
  )
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = brk, cf_piecewise = cf_pw)
}

pw_river <- piecewise_cf_row("River water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "River water"), L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use)
pw_sed   <- piecewise_cf_row("Sediment",    dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Sediment"),    L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed)
pw_ocean <- piecewise_cf_row("Ocean water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Ocean water"), L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean)

# Piecewise sensitivity is an exposure-only (CF/EED) effect: apply the single
# piecewise CF point estimate to the raw per-sample measured concentrations,
# then bootstrap the EED exactly as for the single-slope case. Hazard (haz*)
# is unchanged, so any RQ shift below is attributable to the piecewise CF alone.
set.seed(9401)
eed_boot_piecewise_river <- if (is.finite(pw_river$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring$C_measured_pL * pw_river$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL

Bounding range interpretation. The table above states, per matrix, the single-slope production RQ alongside the piecewise-sensitivity RQ; whichever is larger sets the upper bound of the sensitivity range and whichever is smaller sets the lower bound. Because the fine-size (sub-break) slope from the §13.2 diagnostic is shallower than the coarse-size slope for the matrices where the two-segment model is favored, the piecewise CF is expected to sit below the single-slope CF (less extrapolated mass assigned to the unconstrained 1 um-LOD_low zone) — i.e., the piecewise bound is expected to narrow the exposure (and therefore RQ) estimate relative to the single-slope production value, not widen it, for this dataset. This is stated as an expectation to be read against the rendered numbers above, not assumed; if a matrix’s piecewise CF instead exceeds the single-slope CF, that reversal is itself informative about how sensitive the conclusion is to the extrapolation model and should be flagged rather than averaged away. Regardless of direction, the single-slope CF remains the production default per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec; the piecewise result is reported here strictly as a labeled sensitivity bound. Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d): the Sediment column/row above is illustrative only, for the same reason noted in Section 13.1/11.3.0 — its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value.

The Sediment row is retained here for completeness but is illustrative/non-quantitative (SPEC 1d, Section 11.3.0/11.4.0): its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value, so it must not be read alongside the River water and Ocean water rows as a comparable risk finding.

12.5 Methods-robustness and source-attribution analyses (surface water only)

Three additive analyses testing whether the risk conclusion is robust to specific methodological choices (the sub-floor extrapolation, the extrapolation model itself), and whether the river-vs-ocean slope difference has independent support from polymer composition. River and ocean only — sediment is not touched. None of these change the production headline (single-slope C-PSD, L_tar_min = 1 µm); each is a clearly-labeled sensitivity/robustness addition that reuses the already-computed production hazard/exposure objects wherever possible rather than recomputing them.

12.5.1 RQ sensitivity to the extrapolation floor L_tar_min (food dilution)

The production correction factor extrapolates the measured particle count down to L_tar_min = 1 µm. Food Dilution is volume-weighted, so a power-law explosion of sub-floor particle number adds little particle volume — the RQ may be far less sensitive to L_tar_min than the raw number-based CF implies. This test is only valid if exposure and hazard are evaluated on the same lower size bound, so for each floor the toxicity dataset is filtered to match: a ToMEx record is excluded from a given floor if its own characteristic tested size (size.length.um.used.for.conversions for monodisperse records, or the tested range via size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions for polydisperse records — the same field PSSDplusplus::align_data() itself uses to size-align doses) falls entirely below that floor. Records with a missing characteristic size are excluded rather than imputed. filter_tox_by_size_floor() (R/mp_risk_utils.R) implements this rule.

At each floor, three things move together: (1) the exposure-side correction factor and EED are recomputed over [L_tar_min, 5000] µm; (2) the pSSD++ integration floor (x1M_set in matrix_function(), x1D_set in run_pssd_pipeline()) is set to the same L_tar_min; and (3) the Food Dilution toxicity records are filtered as above before the hazard alignment is re-derived. The L_tar_min = 1 µm row reuses the already-computed production CF/EED/hazard objects rather than recomputing an identical result under a new seed (relocate-don’t-recompute).

Show the code 
m12_floors <- c(1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 20)

m12_run_one_floor <- function(L_tar_min, matrix_label, monitoring_df, cpsd_fit, alpha_draws,
                               tox_data_base, param_values_base, environments,
                               matrix_extra_args, rave_override_fn, seed_base,
                               prod_cf = NULL, prod_eed = NULL, prod_haz = NULL) {

  tox_data_i  <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_base, L_tar_min)
  n_tox_i     <- nrow(tox_data_i)
  n_species_i <- dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_i$Species)

  na_row <- function(note) {
    tibble::tibble(
      Matrix = matrix_label, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      CF_p50 = NA_real_, EED_q50 = NA_real_,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i, HC5_median = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p025_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p975_1D = NA_real_, P_exceed_1D = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = NA_real_, P_exceed_MC2D = NA_real_,
      CF_RSD_pct = NA_real_, RQ_p50_RSD_pct = NA_real_, note = note
    )
  }

  if (isTRUE(L_tar_min == 1) && !is.null(prod_cf)) {
    combined_cf_i <- prod_cf
    eed_boot_i    <- prod_eed
    haz_i         <- prod_haz
  } else {
    set.seed(seed_base)
    corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
      monitoring = monitoring_df, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit,
      alpha_draws = alpha_draws, L_tar_min = L_tar_min, L_tar_max = 5000,
      n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
    )
    combined_cf_i <- corr_i$combined_cf
    eed_boot_i    <- corr_i$eed_boot

    set.seed(seed_base + 1)
    # matrix_function_safe() (R/mp_risk_utils.R): a local patched copy of
    # PSSDplusplus::matrix_function() -- the installed package's oversample-
    # then-slice logic for upper.tissue.trans.size.um silently under-fills
    # when x1M_set narrows the acceptance window (confirmed failing at
    # x1M_set >= 20 with this analysis's real river parameters); the patch
    # replaces only that block with a draw-until-quota-met loop using the
    # identical rnorm() parameters and filter conditions. See the function's
    # own roxygen comment for the full diagnosis. Installed PSSDplusplus is
    # never modified.
    param_matrix_i <- do.call(
      matrix_function_safe,
      c(list(n_sobol = n_boot, params = param_values_base, upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
             x1M_set = L_tar_min, x2D_set = 5000), matrix_extra_args)
    ) |> rave_override_fn()

    # A high L_tar_min can leave too few (or zero) Food-Dilution-alignable
    # records after PSSDplusplus's own ingestible/size-gating logic runs
    # inside MC_sim_align_parallel(), even when the raw filtered tox_data_i
    # row count looks adequate -- build_haz_df() then has nothing to
    # summarise for that ERM. Caught here rather than crashing the render,
    # per the spec's own guardrail: flag as indicative-only (NA row with a
    # note) rather than treat as a production result.
    pssd_haz <- tryCatch({
      pssd_i <- run_pssd_pipeline(
        tox_data = tox_data_i, param_matrix = param_matrix_i, environments = environments,
        cache_suffix = paste0("m12_", matrix_label, "_", L_tar_min),
        dose_unit = "L", n_sim = n_boot, num_cores = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
        sim = 30, cv_uf = 0.5, rmore_method = "lognormal",
        seed = seed_base + 2, x1D_set = L_tar_min
      )
      haz_try <- build_haz_df(pssd_i$pSSDs, environments[1])
      if (is.null(haz_try) || nrow(haz_try) == 0 ||
          !any(haz_try$ERM == "Food Dilution" & haz_try$HCx == 5)) {
        list(ok = FALSE, note = "pSSD fit returned no Food Dilution HC5 at this floor")
      } else {
        list(ok = TRUE, haz = haz_try)
      }
    }, error = function(e) {
      list(ok = FALSE, note = paste0("pSSD/hazard fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e)))
    })

    if (!pssd_haz$ok) {
      return(na_row(pssd_haz$note))
    }
    haz_i <- pssd_haz$haz
  }

  set.seed(seed_base + 3)
  risk_draws_1d <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_i, eed_boot_i$q50, n_risk = 1000)
  rs_1d <- summarize_rq(risk_draws_1d) |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
  rs_1d_ci <- risk_draws_1d |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                      RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))

  mc2d_i <- mc2d_risk(monitoring_df = monitoring_df, combined_cf = combined_cf_i, haz_df = haz_i,
                       n_uncertainty = 100, n_variability = 500, seed = seed_base + 4)
  mc2d_food_hc5_i <- mc2d_i |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
  rs_mc2d <- mc2d_food_hc5_i |>
    dplyr::summarise(P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed), RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50))

  hc5_i <- haz_i |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()

  # Uncertainty (not variability) at this floor: %RSD of the exposure-side CF
  # draws (correction_factor() output, one value per alpha_draws realization)
  # and %RSD of the outer-loop (uncertainty) RQ_p50 across mc2d_risk()'s
  # n_uncertainty = 100 CF+PNEC draws. Both are dispersion-of-the-estimate
  # measures, not the exposure variability captured by the inner loop --
  # answers "how much does our estimate of the risk move if we re-ran the
  # uncertain inputs," at each L_tar_min.
  cf_rsd_pct     <- 100 * stats::sd(combined_cf_i) / mean(combined_cf_i)
  rq_p50_rsd_pct <- 100 * stats::sd(mc2d_food_hc5_i$RQ_p50) / mean(mc2d_food_hc5_i$RQ_p50)

  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_label, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
    CF_p50 = stats::median(combined_cf_i), EED_q50 = stats::median(eed_boot_i$q50),
    n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i, HC5_median = hc5_i,
    RQ_p50_1D = rs_1d$RQ_p50, RQ_p025_1D = rs_1d_ci$RQ_p025, RQ_p975_1D = rs_1d_ci$RQ_p975, P_exceed_1D = rs_1d$P_exceed,
    RQ_p50_MC2D = rs_mc2d$RQ_p50_med, P_exceed_MC2D = rs_mc2d$P_exceed_med,
    CF_RSD_pct = cf_rsd_pct, RQ_p50_RSD_pct = rq_p50_rsd_pct, note = NA_character_
  )
}

rave_override_river <- function(pm) {
  pm |> dplyr::mutate(
    R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    H_W_ratio.freshwater   = sample(R.ave_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )
}
rave_override_ocean <- function(pm) {
  pm |> dplyr::mutate(
    R.ave.water.marine     = sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    H_W_ratio.water.marine = sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )
}

m12_river_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(m12_floors, function(L) {
  m12_run_one_floor(
    L_tar_min = L, matrix_label = "River water", monitoring_df = monitoring,
    cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_all, alpha_draws = alpha, tox_data_base = tox_data,
    param_values_base = param_values, environments = c("Freshwater"),
    matrix_extra_args = list(), rave_override_fn = rave_override_river,
    seed_base = 61000 + round(L * 10), prod_cf = combined_cf, prod_eed = eed_boot, prod_haz = haz
  )
}))

m12_ocean_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(m12_floors, function(L) {
  m12_run_one_floor(
    L_tar_min = L, matrix_label = "Ocean water", monitoring_df = monitoring_ocean,
    cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_ocean_all, alpha_draws = alpha_ocean, tox_data_base = tox_data_ocean,
    param_values_base = param_values_ocean, environments = c("Marine"),
    matrix_extra_args = list(include_marine_surface_water = TRUE, include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
                              include_marine_sediment = FALSE, include_freshwater_sediment = FALSE),
    rave_override_fn = rave_override_ocean,
    seed_base = 62000 + round(L * 10), prod_cf = combined_cf_ocean, prod_eed = eed_boot_ocean, prod_haz = haz_ocean
  )
}))

Guardrails and interpretation. The L_tar_min = 1 µm row is the production headline and is unchanged by this analysis (reused, not recomputed). Any floor where n_species falls below the pSSD++ practical minimum is indicative only — read n_species in the table above before interpreting that row’s RQ. If the Food Dilution median RQ and P(RQ>1) stay well above 1 across all four floors, the sub-floor extrapolation is not driving the exceedance conclusion (expected, since Food Dilution’s volume-weighted dose model damps the sub-floor particle-number explosion); if the exceedance instead collapses at a higher floor, the conclusion is sensitive to the 1 µm extrapolation and that dependency should be stated plainly rather than averaged away.

12.5.1.1 Does restricting the analysis to sizes closer to the measured range reduce uncertainty?

L_tar_min = 1 µm is the largest extrapolation below the measured detection window (165–385 µm river, 95–245 µm ocean); raising the floor shortens that extrapolation. Two dispersion metrics separate this from the magnitude sensitivity shown above: (1) CF_RSD_pct, the relative standard deviation (%RSD = 100 x SD / mean) of the correction-factor draws themselves (combined_cf_i, one value per alpha_draws realization) – a pure exposure-side uncertainty measure; and (2) RQ_p50_RSD_pct, the %RSD of the median RQ across mc2d_risk()’s n_uncertainty = 100 outer-loop draws (each redrawing one CF and one PNEC) – i.e., how much our estimate of the median RQ itself moves if the uncertain inputs were redrawn, isolated from the inner-loop exposure variability that RQ_p50_MC2D above already integrates over.

# CF %RSD and RQ p50 %RSD live on very different scales, so RQ %RSD is drawn
# against a secondary axis. ggplot2 has no native second y-scale: the
# standard workaround is to rescale the secondary series onto the primary
# series' numeric range by a single ratio, plot it on the primary axis, then
# add a sec_axis() that applies the inverse transform purely for the axis
# labels -- the data themselves are only ever plotted once, in primary units.
m12_rsd_max_cf <- max(m12_results$CF_RSD_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
m12_rsd_max_rq <- max(m12_results$RQ_p50_RSD_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
m12_rsd_ratio  <- m12_rsd_max_cf / m12_rsd_max_rq

m12_rsd_plot_df <- m12_results |>
  dplyr::select(Matrix, L_tar_min, CF_RSD_pct, RQ_p50_RSD_pct) |>
  dplyr::mutate(RQ_p50_RSD_pct_scaled = RQ_p50_RSD_pct * m12_rsd_ratio)

# linetype is mapped to a fixed per-layer string (not a pivoted column) so
# each layer gets its own unambiguous legend key -- a shared/pivoted linetype
# aes previously produced two legend entries that both rendered as solid
# lines because geom_point() (no linetype of its own) was merged into the
# same guide as geom_line().
m12_rsd_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(m12_rsd_plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = L_tar_min, color = Matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = CF_RSD_pct, linetype = "CF (exposure), left axis"),
                      linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(y = CF_RSD_pct), size = 2.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = RQ_p50_RSD_pct_scaled, linetype = "RQ p50 (uncertainty), right axis"),
                      linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(y = RQ_p50_RSD_pct_scaled), size = 2.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("River water" = "#0072B2", "Ocean water" = "#009E73"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("CF (exposure), left axis" = "solid", "RQ p50 (uncertainty), right axis" = "dashed"),
    name = NULL,
    guide = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.1))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    name = "CF %RSD (left axis)",
    sec.axis = ggplot2::sec_axis(~ . / m12_rsd_ratio, name = "RQ p50 %RSD (right axis)")
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = expression(L[tar-min]~"(µm)"),
    title = "Does a higher extrapolation floor reduce estimate uncertainty?",
    subtitle = "Solid = exposure-side CF %RSD (left axis); dashed = Food Dilution HC5 median-RQ %RSD, MC2D uncertainty (outer) loop (right axis)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.8, "cm"),
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4)
  )

m12_rsd_river <- m12_results |> dplyr::filter(Matrix == "River water") |> dplyr::arrange(L_tar_min)
m12_rsd_ocean <- m12_results |> dplyr::filter(Matrix == "Ocean water", !is.na(CF_RSD_pct)) |> dplyr::arrange(L_tar_min)

Interpretation. For river water, CF %RSD moves from 247.9% at L_tar_min = 1 µm to 52% at 20 µm, and RQ p50 %RSD moves from 284.6% to 535.4% over the same range. For ocean water (valid floors only, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 µm), CF %RSD moves from 152.5% to 55.7%, and RQ p50 %RSD from 861.8% to 327.8%. Restricting the correction factor to sizes closer to the measured window does reduce exposure-side dispersion for river water, consistent with a shorter power-law extrapolation carrying less compounded uncertainty. This is a CF/RQ-estimate dispersion result, not a data-availability result: it does not by itself justify raising the production floor above L_tar_min = 1 µm, because (a) the RQ magnitude sensitivity above already shows Food Dilution risk is not being driven by the sub-floor extrapolation, and (b) a higher floor discards real tox and monitoring size range along with the extrapolation, at the species-count cost quantified in Section 12.5.1.2 below and in the n_species column here.

12.5.1.2 Why does the ocean Food Dilution fit fail above L_tar_min = 10 µm?

Show the code 
# Why ocean, not river, loses its Food Dilution fit above L_tar_min = 1 um --
# diagnostic only (not part of the m12_results pipeline above). Answers: is
# this a code bug, or a real property of the marine ToMEx subset? Computed
# from the same tox_data / tox_data_ocean / filter_tox_by_size_floor() the
# m12 pipeline itself uses, so the numbers below stay live.
m12_char_size <- function(d) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    d$polydispersity == "polydisperse" & !is.na(d$size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions) ~
      d$size.length.max.um.used.for.conversions,
    d$polydispersity == "monodisperse" & !is.na(d$size.length.um.used.for.conversions) ~
      d$size.length.um.used.for.conversions,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )
}

m12_diag <- list(
  river_sp1   = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data, 1)$Species),
  river_sp20  = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data, 20)$Species),
  ocean_sp1   = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 1)$Species),
  ocean_sp20  = dplyr::n_distinct(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 20)$Species),
  ocean_fish1  = sum(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 1)$Group  == "Fish"),
  ocean_fish20 = sum(filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, 20)$Group == "Fish"),
  river_med_size = stats::median(m12_char_size(tox_data), na.rm = TRUE),
  ocean_med_size = stats::median(m12_char_size(tox_data_ocean), na.rm = TRUE)
)

Ocean’s larger raw species pool is real (31 marine vs 23 freshwater species pass the same QC filters before any size floor is applied) but it is concentrated at much smaller tested particle sizes: the marine subset’s median characteristic tested size is 5 µm against 21 µm for freshwater, and 80% of marine records are monodisperse (small, uniform test beads) versus 40% for freshwater. Raising the floor to 20 µm therefore removes marine records disproportionately: usable species fall from 23 to 10 for ocean (a 57% drop) versus 19 to 14 for river (26%). Fish records, the single largest marine Food-Dilution-relevant group at 1 µm, collapse from 170 to 1 – almost all marine fish-feeding studies in this ToMEx subset used particles smaller than 20 µm. Once run_pssd_pipeline()’s own ingestibility/dose-positive/non-Algae gating runs on top of that, too few marine species remain for PSSDplusplus to construct a Food Dilution SSD at all at L_tar_min = 20 µm, so pSSDs[["Tier3_Marine_Food Dilution"]] is NULL and the row is flagged NA rather than fabricated – this is a genuine data-sparsity limit of the current marine ToMEx subset at larger size floors, not a pipeline defect. The two finer intermediate floors (5, 10 µm) added below still resolve, confirming the failure is specific to the 20 µm floor rather than a broad breakdown of the marine pipeline.

12.5.1.3 M2 – Decomposition of the M1.2 floor effect

DECOMPOSITION DIAGNOSTIC – NOT A RISK ESTIMATE. Section 12.5.1 varies a single control knob, L_tar_min, and moves three things at once: (1) the exposure correction-factor extrapolation, (2) the pSSD++ hazard-integration range, and (3) which tox records survive filter_tox_by_size_floor() (composition). Because these move together, M1.2 alone cannot attribute the RQ collapse it shows to a mechanism. This section freezes tox composition at a common L_tar_min = 10 µm reference set (tox_fixed) and re-runs the pipeline in two arms that isolate the other two components, then decomposes M1.2’s own total collapse into exposure-CF, hazard-integration, and composition contributions in log-RQ space. No production number is touched; every output here is a labeled diagnostic. Per spec/m2_spec.md’s own caveat: freezing tox at >= 10 µm is mechanistically conservative for Tissue Translocation specifically, since it removes exactly the small (< 83 µm, and especially < 10 µm) particles most translocation-relevant – the TT arm below is a lower bound on TT hazard and a diagnostic contrast, not a TT risk estimate.

Show the code 
TOX_FIXED_FLOOR <- 10 # µm; the highest M1.2 floor at which both river and ocean Food Dilution SSDs still converge (ocean fails at 20 µm) -- a composition-stable set common to every arm.
tox_fixed_river <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data,       TOX_FIXED_FLOOR)
tox_fixed_ocean <- filter_tox_by_size_floor(tox_data_ocean, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR)
m2_floors <- c(1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10) # adds 7.5 µm vs the spec's motivating {1,2.5,5,10} to resolve the 5->10 shoulder; matches m12_floors exactly so M1.2 values need no interpolation.

m2_get_cfg <- function(compartment) {
  if (compartment == "river") {
    list(monitoring_df = monitoring, cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_all, alpha_draws = alpha,
         tox_data_base = tox_data, tox_fixed = tox_fixed_river,
         param_values_base = param_values, environments = c("Freshwater"),
         matrix_extra_args = list(), rave_override_fn = rave_override_river, env_key = "Freshwater",
         prod_cf = combined_cf, prod_eed = eed_boot, prod_haz = haz)
  } else {
    list(monitoring_df = monitoring_ocean, cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_ocean_all, alpha_draws = alpha_ocean,
         tox_data_base = tox_data_ocean, tox_fixed = tox_fixed_ocean,
         param_values_base = param_values_ocean, environments = c("Marine"),
         matrix_extra_args = list(include_marine_surface_water = TRUE, include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
                                   include_marine_sediment = FALSE, include_freshwater_sediment = FALSE),
         rave_override_fn = rave_override_ocean, env_key = "Marine",
         prod_cf = combined_cf_ocean, prod_eed = eed_boot_ocean, prod_haz = haz_ocean)
  }
}

# One pSSD/hazard fit (matrix_function_safe() -> run_pssd_pipeline() -> build_haz_df()),
# tryCatch-wrapped per the M1.2 precedent so a data-insufficient cell reports a
# note instead of crashing the render (spec guardrail: "report the failure
# rather than silently dropping the cell").
m2_compute_hazard <- function(cfg, tox_i, x_haz, cache_tag, seed_hazard) {
  set.seed(seed_hazard)
  param_matrix_i <- do.call(
    matrix_function_safe,
    c(list(n_sobol = n_boot, params = cfg$param_values_base, upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
           x1M_set = x_haz, x2D_set = 5000), cfg$matrix_extra_args)
  ) |> cfg$rave_override_fn()

  tryCatch({
    pssd_i <- run_pssd_pipeline(
      tox_data = tox_i, param_matrix = param_matrix_i, environments = cfg$environments,
      cache_suffix = cache_tag, dose_unit = "L", n_sim = n_boot,
      num_cores = parallel::detectCores() - 2, sim = 30, cv_uf = 0.5, rmore_method = "lognormal",
      seed = seed_hazard, x1D_set = x_haz
    )
    haz_try <- build_haz_df(pssd_i$pSSDs, cfg$env_key)
    if (is.null(haz_try) || nrow(haz_try) == 0) {
      list(ok = FALSE, haz = NULL, note = "pSSD fit returned no hazard rows at this arm/floor")
    } else {
      list(ok = TRUE, haz = haz_try, note = NA_character_)
    }
  }, error = function(e) list(ok = FALSE, haz = NULL, note = paste0("pSSD/hazard fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e))))
}

#' One (compartment, arm, floor) cell of the M2 grid
#'
#' arm "A"        -- composition AND hazard-integration bound frozen at
#'                   TOX_FIXED_FLOOR (tox_fixed, x1M/x1D = 10); only the
#'                   exposure CF floor tracks L_tar_min. Isolates component
#'                   (1), pure exposure-CF/de-extrapolation.
#' arm "B"        -- composition frozen (tox_fixed) but the hazard-integration
#'                   bound now tracks L_tar_min too. Adds component (2),
#'                   hazard-integration-range, on top of Arm A.
#' arm "M12equiv" -- composition ALSO tracks L_tar_min (filter_tox_by_size_floor
#'                   re-applied at every floor), i.e. exactly M1.2's own
#'                   pipeline. Reused directly from the live m12_results object
#'                   for Food Dilution (never recomputed); computed fresh here
#'                   for Tissue Translocation, which M1.2 itself never covered.
m2_run_one <- function(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, seed_exposure, seed_hazard, arm_a_haz_cache) {
  cfg <- m2_get_cfg(compartment)
  tox_i <- if (arm %in% c("A", "B")) cfg$tox_fixed else filter_tox_by_size_floor(cfg$tox_data_base, L_tar_min)
  n_tox_i <- nrow(tox_i)
  n_species_i <- dplyr::n_distinct(tox_i$Species)

  na_row <- function(note) {
    tibble::tibble(
      compartment = compartment, arm = arm, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i,
      CF_p50 = NA_real_, EED_q50 = NA_real_,
      ERM = NA_character_, HC5_median = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p025_1D = NA_real_, RQ_p975_1D = NA_real_, P_exceed_1D = NA_real_,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = NA_real_, P_exceed_MC2D = NA_real_, note = note,
      risk_draws_1d = list(NULL)
    )
  }

  # Exposure: seed is a function of (compartment, floor) ONLY -- shared across
  # all three arms (m2-grid-run below), never varying by arm, because CF/EED
  # computation is identical logic for every arm (all three track L_tar_min on
  # the exposure side; only the hazard side differs). This is required for
  # M2.1's paired study-inclusion-effect companion panel (Section 12.5.1.3.1):
  # the paired ratio RQ_M12,i/RQ_ArmB,i = HC5_ArmB,i/HC5_M12,i only holds if
  # E_i (exposure draw i) is literally the same value for Arm B and M12equiv
  # at every Monte Carlo index i. No "relocate, don't recompute" shortcut at
  # L_tar_min = 1 here (unlike M1.2's own floor=1 reuse) -- reusing the
  # separately-seeded production EED at that floor would break the pairing
  # exactly where the headline finding lives.
  set.seed(seed_exposure)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = cfg$monitoring_df, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = cfg$cpsd_fit,
    alpha_draws = cfg$alpha_draws, L_tar_min = L_tar_min, L_tar_max = 5000,
    n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95), slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  combined_cf_i <- corr_i$combined_cf
  eed_boot_i    <- corr_i$eed_boot

  if (arm == "A") {
    # Arm A's hazard is floor-invariant by construction (fixed tox, fixed
    # x1M/x1D = TOX_FIXED_FLOOR regardless of L_tar_min) -- computed once per
    # compartment (below) and reused here, both as a compute-cost saving and
    # as the mechanism that makes Arm A's HC5 bit-identical across floors
    # (acceptance check 2, verified below).
    haz_result <- arm_a_haz_cache[[compartment]]
  } else {
    haz_result <- m2_compute_hazard(
      cfg, tox_i, x_haz = L_tar_min,
      cache_tag = paste0("m2_", compartment, "_", arm, "_", L_tar_min),
      seed_hazard = seed_hazard
    )
  }
  if (!haz_result$ok) return(na_row(haz_result$note))
  haz_i <- haz_result$haz

  # Same shared-seed principle applies to the E-side resampling inside
  # draw_rq_mc1d(): seeding identically (seed_exposure + 1, shared across
  # arms) before each arm's call, given identical eed_boot_i$q50 inputs and
  # identical (ERM, HCx) group iteration order (dplyr::group_by() sorts
  # alphabetically), produces identical E_i draws per ERM group across arms.
  # draw_idx retains draw order so the companion panel can pair rows exactly.
  set.seed(seed_exposure + 1)
  risk_draws_1d <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_i, eed_boot_i$q50, n_risk = 1000) |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::mutate(draw_idx = dplyr::row_number()) |>
    dplyr::ungroup()

  rs_1d <- risk_draws_1d |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      RQ_p50  = stats::median(RQ), P_exceed = mean(RQ > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
      RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  # mc2d_risk() resamples the already-computed combined_cf_i/haz_i (no new
  # pSSD fit), so this is cheap relative to the hazard fit above -- included
  # per the spec's Table M2-1 ("Arm A RQ (1D + MC2D med)") and M2.1's caveat 2
  # (metric dependence: the 1D "<1" statement must be checked under MC2D too).
  set.seed(seed_exposure + 2)
  mc2d_i <- mc2d_risk(monitoring_df = cfg$monitoring_df, combined_cf = combined_cf_i, haz_df = haz_i,
                       n_uncertainty = 100, n_variability = 500, seed = seed_exposure + 2)
  rs_mc2d <- mc2d_i |> dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p50_MC2D = stats::median(RQ_p50), P_exceed_MC2D = stats::median(P_exceed), .groups = "drop")

  hc5_by_erm <- haz_i |> dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(HC5_median = stats::median(PNEC), .groups = "drop")

  # risk_draws_1d nested as a per-ERM list-column so the companion panel
  # (Section 12.5.1.3.1) can unnest and pair Arm B / M12equiv draws by
  # (compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, draw_idx) without any new pSSD computation.
  draws_nested <- risk_draws_1d |> dplyr::group_by(ERM) |> tidyr::nest() |> dplyr::rename(risk_draws_1d = data)

  rs_1d |>
    dplyr::left_join(hc5_by_erm, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::left_join(rs_mc2d, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::left_join(draws_nested, by = "ERM") |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      compartment = compartment, arm = arm, L_tar_min = L_tar_min,
      n_tox_records = n_tox_i, n_species = n_species_i,
      CF_p50 = stats::median(combined_cf_i), EED_q50 = stats::median(eed_boot_i$q50),
      ERM = ERM, HC5_median = HC5_median,
      RQ_p50_1D = RQ_p50, RQ_p025_1D = RQ_p025, RQ_p975_1D = RQ_p975, P_exceed_1D = P_exceed,
      RQ_p50_MC2D = RQ_p50_MC2D, P_exceed_MC2D = P_exceed_MC2D, note = NA_character_,
      risk_draws_1d = risk_draws_1d
    )
}
Show the code 
arm_a_haz_cache <- list(
  river = m2_compute_hazard(m2_get_cfg("river"), tox_fixed_river, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "m2_armA_haz_river", seed_hazard = 81011),
  ocean = m2_compute_hazard(m2_get_cfg("ocean"), tox_fixed_ocean, TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "m2_armA_haz_ocean", seed_hazard = 81021)
)

m2_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  compartment = c("river", "ocean"),
  arm         = c("A", "B", "M12equiv"),
  L_tar_min   = m2_floors
)

m2_results <- purrr::pmap_dfr(m2_grid, function(compartment, arm, L_tar_min) {
  comp_idx  <- match(compartment, c("river", "ocean"))
  arm_idx   <- match(arm, c("A", "B", "M12equiv"))
  floor_idx <- match(L_tar_min, m2_floors)
  # seed_exposure deliberately excludes arm_idx (shared across arms -- see the
  # m2-harness chunk's comment on why Arm B / M12equiv need identical E draws).
  seed_exposure <- 81000 + comp_idx * 10000 + floor_idx * 10
  seed_hazard   <- 81000 + comp_idx * 10000 + arm_idx * 1000 + floor_idx * 10 + 1
  m2_run_one(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, seed_exposure, seed_hazard, arm_a_haz_cache)
})
Show the code 
# Food Dilution M1.2 reference: read the ALREADY-RENDERED, live M1.2 result
# directly from m12_results (Section 12.5.1) -- never re-derived, per the
# spec's explicit "do not re-run M1.2" instruction and this document's
# no-retyped-literals convention. Tissue Translocation has no M1.2 curve in
# this document (M1.2 was scoped to Food Dilution only, per its own spec), so
# for TT the "M1.2-equivalent" reference is M2's own tox-tracking M12equiv
# arm. Carries the RQ point estimate + 1D 95% CI + MC2D median so the
# scenario figure (Section 12.5.1.3.1) and the decomposition (Section
# 12.5.1.3.5) both draw from one function instead of two separate constructions.
bind_m12_reference <- function() {
  fd <- m12_results |>
    dplyr::filter(L_tar_min %in% m2_floors, is.na(note)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      compartment = ifelse(Matrix == "River water", "river", "ocean"),
      ERM = "Food Dilution", L_tar_min,
      RQ_p50 = RQ_p50_1D, RQ_lo = RQ_p025_1D, RQ_hi = RQ_p975_1D, RQ_mc2d = RQ_p50_MC2D, HC5 = HC5_median
    )
  tt <- m2_results |>
    dplyr::filter(arm == "M12equiv", ERM == "Tissue Translocation", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min,
                      RQ_p50 = RQ_p50_1D, RQ_lo = RQ_p025_1D, RQ_hi = RQ_p975_1D, RQ_mc2d = RQ_p50_MC2D, HC5 = HC5_median)
  dplyr::bind_rows(fd, tt)
}

m12_ref_full <- bind_m12_reference()
m12_ref <- m12_ref_full |> dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_m12 = RQ_p50)

arm_a_ref <- m2_results |> dplyr::filter(arm == "A", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_A = RQ_p50_1D)
arm_b_ref <- m2_results |> dplyr::filter(arm == "B", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min, RQ_B = RQ_p50_1D)

m2_panel_labels <- c(river = "River", ocean = "Ocean")
Show the code 
# Three-way decomposition, computed here (data only -- Table M2-2 and the
# fold-contribution table are DISPLAYED later, in the relegated Section
# 12.5.1.3.5, but the underlying numbers are needed by the PROMOTED
# interpretation in 12.5.1.3.1 too, so the arithmetic lives in one place):
#   dlogRQ_total(f)       = logRQ_M1.2(f)  - logRQ_M1.2(10)   [[from the live M1.2/M12equiv reference]]
#   dlogRQ_exposureCF(f)  = logRQ_ArmA(f)  - logRQ_ArmA(10)   [[pure exposure-CF/de-extrapolation]]
#   dlogRQ_hazardInteg(f) = logRQ_ArmB(f)  - logRQ_ArmA(f)    [[hazard-integration-range effect]]
#   dlogRQ_composition(f) = logRQ_M1.2(f)  - logRQ_ArmB(f)    [[study-filtration/composition residual]]
m2_decomp <- m12_ref |>
  dplyr::inner_join(arm_a_ref, by = c("compartment", "ERM", "L_tar_min")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(arm_b_ref, by = c("compartment", "ERM", "L_tar_min")) |>
  dplyr::filter(RQ_m12 > 0, RQ_A > 0, RQ_B > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(logRQ_m12 = log10(RQ_m12), logRQ_A = log10(RQ_A), logRQ_B = log10(RQ_B)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(compartment, ERM) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    logRQ_m12_ref = logRQ_m12[L_tar_min == TOX_FIXED_FLOOR][1],
    logRQ_A_ref   = logRQ_A[L_tar_min == TOX_FIXED_FLOOR][1]
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dlogRQ_total       = logRQ_m12 - logRQ_m12_ref,
    dlogRQ_exposureCF  = logRQ_A - logRQ_A_ref,
    dlogRQ_hazardInteg = logRQ_B - logRQ_A,
    dlogRQ_composition = logRQ_m12 - logRQ_B,
    residual           = dlogRQ_total - (dlogRQ_exposureCF + dlogRQ_hazardInteg + dlogRQ_composition)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-logRQ_m12_ref, -logRQ_A_ref)

# fold_* = 10^(dlogRQ) directly (NOT negated): dlogRQ_total(1) = logRQ(1) -
# logRQ(10), and RQ(1) >> RQ(10) (RQ collapses as the floor rises), so
# dlogRQ_total(1) is large and POSITIVE -- 10^(dlogRQ_total) > 1 correctly
# represents "RQ is this many times higher at 1 µm than at 10 µm," i.e. the
# collapse magnitude the spec's motivating "~100-130x" language means.
m2_fold_summary <- m2_decomp |>
  dplyr::filter(L_tar_min == min(m2_floors)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    fold_total       = 10^(dlogRQ_total),
    fold_exposureCF  = 10^(dlogRQ_exposureCF),
    fold_hazardInteg = 10^(dlogRQ_hazardInteg),
    fold_composition = 10^(dlogRQ_composition)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, ERM, fold_total, fold_exposureCF, fold_hazardInteg, fold_composition)

12.5.1.3.1 Study inclusion, not sub-10 µm extrapolation, drives the exceedance

Two of M2’s three arms are size-coherent – exposure and hazard are rescaled together to the identical [L_tar_min, 5000] µm range at every floor – and their difference isolates the study-inclusion (composition) effect cleanly, with no size-basis mismatch: Arm B (tox composition frozen at 10 µm; only which studies are SSD members is held fixed) versus M1.2/M12equiv (tox composition also tracks the floor, i.e. exactly the production/M1.2 pipeline). Arm A does not appear here – see Section 12.5.1.3.5 for why its absolute values are not physically meaningful on their own.

Show the code 
scenario_levels <- c("Study set fixed (>=10 µm tox)", "Study set tracks floor (production)")

m2_scenario_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  m2_results |> dplyr::filter(arm == "B", !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
    dplyr::transmute(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min,
                      RQ_p50 = RQ_p50_1D, RQ_lo = RQ_p025_1D, RQ_hi = RQ_p975_1D,
                      RQ_mc2d = RQ_p50_MC2D, HC5 = HC5_median, scenario = scenario_levels[1]),
  m12_ref_full |> dplyr::mutate(scenario = scenario_levels[2])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, levels = scenario_levels))

# Paired study-inclusion effect (companion panel): Arm B and M12equiv share
# IDENTICAL exposure draws at each (compartment, floor) -- the m2-harness
# chunk seeds correct_and_bootstrap_eed() and draw_rq_mc1d()'s E-sampling
# identically across arms for exactly this reason -- so pairing by draw_idx
# cancels the exposure term exactly:
#   RQ_M12,i / RQ_ArmB,i = (E_i / H_M12,i) / (E_i / H_ArmB,i) = H_ArmB,i / H_M12,i
m2_paired_draws <- m2_results |>
  dplyr::filter(arm %in% c("B", "M12equiv"), !is.na(RQ_p50_1D)) |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, ERM, risk_draws_1d) |>
  tidyr::unnest(risk_draws_1d)

paired_ratio_df <- m2_paired_draws |>
  dplyr::select(compartment, arm, L_tar_min, ERM, draw_idx, H) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = H, names_prefix = "H_") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(H_B), !is.na(H_M12equiv)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ratio = H_B / H_M12equiv) |>
  dplyr::group_by(compartment, ERM, L_tar_min) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    ratio_p50  = stats::median(ratio),
    ratio_p025 = stats::quantile(ratio, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
    ratio_p975 = stats::quantile(ratio, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_paired   = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

With both exposure and hazard rescaled coherently to a common [L_tar_min, 5000] µm range but the toxicity study set held fixed (Arm B), the river Food Dilution RQ at a 1 µm exposure floor is 0.633 (1D) – below 1. Allowing the study set to open as the floor drops (M12/production) collapses the Food Dilution HC5 from ~918 to ~68 and raises the RQ to 9.403. The 1 µm-floor exceedance is therefore created by admitting <10 µm-tested studies into the food-dilution SSD (a hazard/HC5 effect), not by coherent sub-10 µm extrapolation. Magnitude vs threshold-crossing. Sub-10 µm exposure de-extrapolation is not negligible – it is the larger single lever by magnitude (river Food Dilution exposure-CF fold 79.86x vs composition fold 14.86x). It fails to cross 1 only because it operates on a fixed >=10 µm study set with a very low baseline RQ. Read this as “study inclusion is decisive for threshold-crossing,” never as “extrapolation is irrelevant.” Metric dependence. The clean “<1 without study inclusion” statement is strictly true in 1D for the river; under MC2D the river Arm B Food Dilution RQ is 0.986 versus M12’s 12.383. Ocean Arm B stays <= 1 under both metrics (ocean Arm B 1D = 0.627, MC2D = 0.326). This is a pre-registered hypothesis test (spec/m2_spec.md Section 4.1; reframed for presentation by spec/m21.md), not a tuned conclusion – the rendered numbers above are reported regardless of which way they fall. Tissue Translocation’s M12equiv reference (computed fresh here, since M1.2 itself never covered TT) carries the >= 10 µm composition-freeze caveat throughout: it is a lower bound on TT hazard, not a TT risk estimate. Mechanistically, food dilution is a large-particle (volume/gut-filling) mechanism while small particles preferentially drive translocation (Section 12.5.1’s M1.1 framing); admitting small-particle studies into the volume-based food-dilution SSD is the plausible reason the HC5 collapses when the study set is allowed to track the floor, though this analysis tests the effect, not that specific mechanism, directly.

Figure. The Food Dilution risk exceedance is created by toxicity-study inclusion, not by sub-10 µm size extrapolation. Median Food Dilution risk quotient (RQ, 1D) versus the lower size floor L_tar_min, faceted by compartment; points = median, bars = 95% CI (2.5th-97.5th percentile of the 1D risk draws); dashed line RQ = 1. Blue (“study set fixed >=10 µm”) rescales exposure and hazard coherently to [L_tar_min, 5000] µm but holds SSD membership fixed; orange (“study set tracks floor”) is the production/M1.2 pipeline, which additionally admits studies tested below the floor. Both scenarios rise as the floor decreases – that shared rise is coherent size extrapolation, present in both. The effect of interest is the vertical gap between the curves: at a 1 µm floor the river RQ is 0.633 with the study set fixed but 9.403 when it tracks the floor (a 15x study-inclusion effect), because the food-dilution HC5 collapses from ~918 to ~68 particles/L when <10 µm-tested studies enter the SSD. Coherent extrapolation alone leaves the river RQ below 1 (1D); under MC2D the fixed-set river RQ is 0.986, ~12.6x below the tracking scenario. Diagnostic of model behavior – the production risk characterization is unchanged.

12.5.1.3.2 Why Arm A’s absolute values don’t matter: the HC5-cancellation identity

Because the exposure-CF term is a difference of two Arm-A quantities that share the identical pinned HC5 (Arm A’s hazard is computed once per compartment and reused at every floor – Section 12.5.1.3.5’s acceptance check 2), the HC5 divides out algebraically: ΔlogRQ_exposureCF(f) = log₁₀[EED(f)/EED(10)]. Arm A’s non-physical absolute RQ (exposure and hazard deliberately aligned to different size ranges) never survives this subtraction – only a pure exposure ratio does.

Verified against the raw exposure: river Food Dilution EED q50 is 662.011 at 1 µm and 7.685 at 10 µm – a ratio of 86.1x, matching the reported exposure-CF fold (79.9x, Section 12.5.1.3.5) within Monte Carlo noise (ΔlogRQ_exposureCF = 1.902 at the 1 µm river Food Dilution cell).

12.5.1.3.5 Sub-decomposition of the coherent trajectory (supplementary)

Arm A is a diagnostic device only. Its absolute RQ is non-physical (exposure and hazard are deliberately aligned to different size ranges: exposure over [L_tar_min, 5000] but hazard pinned to [10, 5000]). It appears in the decomposition below solely as the difference ΔlogRQ_exposureCF = logRQ_A(f) − logRQ_A(10), in which the pinned HC5 cancels exactly (Section 12.5.1.3.2), leaving a pure exposure ratio. It is never a risk estimate. Retained in full here, under this explicit flag, for auditability.

# Note: because dlogRQ_exposureCF + dlogRQ_hazardInteg + dlogRQ_composition
# telescopes algebraically to (logRQ_m12 - logRQ_A_ref), the "residual" above
# is exactly (logRQ_A_ref - logRQ_m12_ref) within each compartment x ERM group
# -- i.e. it IS the freeze-point coincidence gap (acceptance check 1), not a
# separate quantity. Both are reported because the spec calls for both, but
# they are not independent evidence of harness correctness.
Show the code 
if (is_production_budget) {
  m2_max_resid <- max(abs(m2_decomp$residual), na.rm = TRUE)
  m2_tol <- 0.3 # log10 units (~2x); generous for independently-seeded MC noise, tight enough to catch a genuine multi-order-of-magnitude wiring error
  cat("M2 acceptance checks (production budget, n_boot =", n_boot, "):\n")
  cat("  Check 1 (freeze-point coincidence) & check 3 (decomposition closure) share one quantity here (see note above): max|residual| =",
      signif(m2_max_resid, 3), "log10 units (tolerance", m2_tol, ").\n")
  stopifnot(
    "M2 acceptance checks 1/3 FAILED: freeze-point coincidence / decomposition closure residual exceeds tolerance -- see m2_decomp" =
      m2_max_resid < m2_tol
  )
  cat("M2 acceptance checks 1 and 3 passed.\n")
} else {
  message("M2 acceptance checks 1 and 3 (freeze-point coincidence, decomposition closure) skipped: dev-scale render (n_boot = ",
          n_boot, " < 1000); MC noise is too large relative to the tolerance at this budget. Re-check at the production budget.")
}

# Check 4 (sign sanity, spec Section 2.5): the spec states "exposure-CF
# component should be negative ... RQ falls as floor rises." Under THIS
# section's delta-vs-10-µm-reference parameterization (dlogRQ_exposureCF(f) =
# logRQ_A(f) - logRQ_A(10)), "RQ falls as floor rises" means RQ_A(f) > RQ_A(10)
# for every floor f < 10 µm (more sub-floor extrapolation at a lower floor ->
# higher CF -> higher EED -> higher RQ, holding hazard fixed as Arm A does) --
# i.e. dlogRQ_exposureCF(f) should be POSITIVE for f < 10, not negative; the
# spec's "negative" describes the trend as the floor itself increases, not
# the sign in this fixed-reference-point delta. Reported, not gated (the
# spec constrains this component's sign informationally; only composition's
# sign is explicitly left unconstrained -- but forcing a stopifnot() here
# would just be re-deriving arithmetic already guaranteed by
# correction_factor()'s own monotonicity, not new evidence about the harness).
m2_sign_check <- m2_decomp |>
  dplyr::filter(L_tar_min != TOX_FIXED_FLOOR) |>
  dplyr::summarise(frac_expected_sign = mean(dlogRQ_exposureCF > 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
cat("Sign sanity: exposure-CF component has the expected sign (RQ_A(f) > RQ_A(10) for f <", TOX_FIXED_FLOOR, "µm) for",
    scales::percent(m2_sign_check$frac_expected_sign, accuracy = 1), "of non-reference rows.\n")

Guardrails. No production headline number is affected by this section (M2 reuses the same underlying correct_and_bootstrap_eed() / matrix_function_safe() / run_pssd_pipeline() / mc2d_risk() functions M1.2 already uses, in new diagnostic configurations; it does not modify the production L_tar_min = 1, fully-tracking pipeline). Arm A deliberately mismatches the exposure and hazard size bases – every Arm A number above is a diagnostic, not a valid stand-alone risk quotient; Arm B numbers, by contrast, are legitimate size-coherent risk quotients (just not the production headline, since composition is deliberately held fixed). Sediment is not touched.

12.5.2 Model-selection robustness: MLE and a tapered/lognormal small-end model

Distinct from Section 4.1’s method-choice statement: this section does not ask whether C-PSD is the right method (it is; Segur et al. 2026 already established C-PSD ≈ MLE in accuracy). It asks how much the risk result depends on the sub-floor extrapolation model, given Segur et al.’s own caveat that C-PSD extrapolates below the measured range, and marine-surface literature suggesting the true small-end particle-size distribution may roll off (fewer small particles than a single power law implies) rather than continue as one power law to 1 µm.

Three models are fit to each matrix’s pooled (“all” shapes) particle-length data: (a) the production C-PSD OLS fit (carried through for comparison, not refit here); (b) an MLE power law (poweRlaw::conpl), with xmin chosen by minimizing the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic and a goodness-of-fit bootstrap p-value (Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009; power law rejected if p < 0.1); and (c) a lognormal small-end alternative (poweRlaw::conlnorm) fit at the same xmin as the MLE power law, compared to it via a Vuong likelihood-ratio test (compare_distributions()). Ocean fiber (5 populated C-PSD bins; Section 12.1.1) is excluded from MLE fitting as too sparse for a stable tail fit.

Show the code 
m13_fit_one_matrix <- function(length_vec, matrix_label, seed) {
  length_vec <- length_vec[is.finite(length_vec) & length_vec > 0]

  m_pl <- poweRlaw::conpl$new(length_vec)
  est  <- poweRlaw::estimate_xmin(m_pl)
  m_pl$setXmin(est)

  set.seed(seed)
  bp <- poweRlaw::bootstrap_p(m_pl, no_of_sims = 100, threads = 1, seed = seed)

  m_ln <- poweRlaw::conlnorm$new(length_vec)
  m_ln$setXmin(m_pl$getXmin())
  m_ln$setPars(poweRlaw::estimate_pars(m_ln))

  comp <- poweRlaw::compare_distributions(m_pl, m_ln)

  list(
    matrix_label = matrix_label,
    n_total = length(length_vec),
    xmin = est$xmin, ntail = est$ntail, alpha_mle = m_pl$pars,
    KS_D = est$gof, bootstrap_p = bp$p,
    meanlog = m_ln$pars[1], sdlog = m_ln$pars[2],
    vuong_stat = comp$test_statistic, vuong_p = comp$p_two_sided
  )
}

m13_river_fit <- m13_fit_one_matrix(raw_particles_river$length_um, "River water", seed = 71001)
m13_ocean_fit <- m13_fit_one_matrix(raw_particles_ocean$length_um, "Ocean water", seed = 71002)

m13_fit_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(list(m13_river_fit, m13_ocean_fit), function(f) {
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = f$matrix_label, n_total = f$n_total, xmin_um = round(f$xmin, 1), n_tail = f$ntail,
    alpha_MLE = round(f$alpha_mle, 3), KS_D = round(f$KS_D, 4), bootstrap_p = round(f$bootstrap_p, 3),
    power_law_rejected = f$bootstrap_p < 0.1,
    vuong_stat = round(f$vuong_stat, 3), vuong_p = round(f$vuong_p, 3),
    lognormal_meanlog = round(f$meanlog, 3), lognormal_sdlog = round(f$sdlog, 3)
  )
}))

)

Show the code 
# Convert each model to an equivalent correction factor over the SAME measured
# window already used for the production C-PSD correction factor
# (L_meas_min_use/L_meas_max_use), so only the extrapolation MODEL differs,
# not the physical measurement window -- then recompute the RQ for both ERMs
# against the already-computed production hazard (haz/haz_ocean; hazard is
# not re-derived here, only the exposure-side extrapolation model changes).
m13_propagate_one <- function(fit, L_meas_min, L_meas_max, monitoring_df, conc_col,
                               haz_df, n_risk, cpsd_a_psd, combined_cf_prod, seed_base) {

  cf_mle <- correction_factor(
    a = -fit$alpha_mle, L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  cf_lognormal <- (stats::plnorm(5000, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog) - stats::plnorm(1, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog)) /
    (stats::plnorm(L_meas_max, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog) - stats::plnorm(L_meas_min, fit$meanlog, fit$sdlog))

  rq_for_cf <- function(cf_val, seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    eed_i <- bootstrap_eed(monitoring_df[[conc_col]] * cf_val, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
    set.seed(seed + 1)
    summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz_df, eed_i$q50, n_risk = n_risk)) |>
      dplyr::filter(ERM %in% c("Food Dilution", "Tissue Translocation"), HCx == 5) |>
      dplyr::select(ERM, RQ_p50, P_exceed)
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(
    rq_for_cf(median(combined_cf_prod), seed_base)     |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "C-PSD (production)", CF = median(combined_cf_prod)),
    rq_for_cf(cf_mle, seed_base + 10)                   |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "MLE power law", CF = cf_mle),
    rq_for_cf(cf_lognormal, seed_base + 20)              |> dplyr::mutate(Model = "Lognormal (tapered small-end)", CF = cf_lognormal)
  ) |> dplyr::mutate(Matrix = fit$matrix_label)
}

m13_river_rq <- m13_propagate_one(
  m13_river_fit, L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use, monitoring, "C_measured_pL",
  haz, n_risk, cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, combined_cf, seed_base = 72001
)
m13_ocean_rq <- m13_propagate_one(
  m13_ocean_fit, L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean, monitoring_ocean, "C_measured_pL",
  haz_ocean, n_risk_ocean, cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_psd, combined_cf_ocean, seed_base = 72002
)

m13_rq_results <- dplyr::bind_rows(m13_river_rq, m13_ocean_rq) |>
  dplyr::relocate(Matrix, Model, ERM, CF, RQ_p50, P_exceed)

Guardrails and interpretation. The C-PSD single-slope fit remains the production default; MLE and lognormal are labeled comparators only, and hazard is never re-derived in this section (only the exposure-side extrapolation model changes, holding haz/haz_ocean fixed at their production values). Report GoF failures honestly: the power law is NOT rejected for river water, and is NOT rejected for ocean water (bootstrap p = 0.25 river, 0.8 ocean). The Vuong test indicates whether the power law and lognormal are statistically distinguishable at each matrix’s shared xmin (p < 0.05 favors one model over the other; a non-significant result means the data cannot discriminate between them at this sample size). If the Food Dilution exceedance conclusion holds across all three models, the risk result is robust to the extrapolation-model choice; if it flips under the lognormal small-end model, that sensitivity should be stated plainly.

12.5.3 River vs ocean polymer composition: test for buoyant-polymer enrichment

A shift in polymer mix at the sea surface — specifically enrichment of buoyant polymers (PP, PE) relative to rivers — would independently support a surface-retention/transport interpretation of the shallower ocean particle-length PSD slope (Section 12.1.1), rather than a source/residence or fitting-window explanation. buoyancy_freshwater/buoyancy_marine are already assigned per particle by assign_polymer_density() (Section 3.1.1), relative to freshwater (1.00 g/cm³) and seawater (1.025 g/cm³) respectively, so no new density-assignment code is needed here — only the statistical test.

Show the code 
# sample_depth_general is entirely NA for every ocean-water particle in this
# study (all 6 ocean sample IDs; confirmed below) -- these µFTIR runs simply
# did not record a depth stratum for ocean grabs, unlike river water, which
# has both strata. Ocean is therefore its own "depth not recorded" level
# rather than being assumed to be "surface" -- no depth label is fabricated
# for data that was not collected with one.
m14_particles <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  raw_particles_river |> dplyr::mutate(Matrix = "River water"),
  raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::mutate(Matrix = "Ocean water")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Depth = dplyr::case_when(
      Matrix == "Ocean water" ~ "depth not recorded",
      TRUE ~ as.character(sample_depth_general)
    )
  )

m14_ocean_depth_recorded <- sum(!is.na(raw_particles_ocean$sample_depth_general))

# Fisher's exact if any expected cell count is small (chi-square approximation
# becomes unreliable below ~5 expected per cell); chi-square otherwise.
m14_expected_min <- suppressWarnings(min(chisq.test(m14_contingency)$expected))
m14_full_test <- if (m14_expected_min < 5) {
  fisher.test(m14_contingency, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)
} else {
  chisq.test(m14_contingency)
}
cat(
  "Full polymer x matrix test:", m14_full_test$method,
  "-- statistic =", if (!is.null(m14_full_test$statistic)) signif(m14_full_test$statistic, 4) else NA,
  ", p =", signif(m14_full_test$p.value, 4),
  "(min expected cell count =", round(m14_expected_min, 2), ")\n"
)
Full polymer x matrix test: Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data with simulated p-value
     (based on 10000 replicates) -- statistic = NA , p = 0.08719 (min expected cell count = 0.18 )
Show the code 
# Focused 2x2 test: buoyant (PP + PE) vs non-buoyant, river vs ocean. PP and PE
# are the only two polymer groups classified "buoyant" under both
# buoyancy_freshwater and buoyancy_marine in this dataset (verified below),
# so "buoyant" here is defined directly by polymer identity rather than by
# picking one of the two medium-specific buoyancy columns.
m14_particles <- m14_particles |>
  dplyr::mutate(is_buoyant = polymer_density_group %in% c("polyethylene", "polypropylene"))

m14_buoyancy_agreement <- mean(m14_particles$buoyancy_freshwater == m14_particles$buoyancy_marine)

m14_2x2 <- table(m14_particles$is_buoyant, m14_particles$Matrix)
m14_2x2_test <- if (min(suppressWarnings(chisq.test(m14_2x2)$expected)) < 5) {
  fisher.test(m14_2x2)
} else {
  chisq.test(m14_2x2, correct = TRUE)
}

m14_buoyant_fraction <- m14_particles |>
  dplyr::group_by(Matrix) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    n_buoyant = sum(is_buoyant),
    fraction_buoyant = n_buoyant / n,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ci = list(stats::binom.test(n_buoyant, n)$conf.int),
    ci_low  = ci[1],
    ci_high = ci[2]
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-ci)

Interpretation. A significant enrichment of PP/PE in ocean surface water relative to river water (36.8% vs 27.0%, 2×2 test p = 0.0327) would support the transport/retention reading of the river-vs-ocean slope difference; a null result points instead toward a source/residence or fitting-window explanation. Caveats. Composition is count-based over each matrix’s own measured detection window (the same LOD/window caveats that apply to the slope fits themselves), and ocean n = 117 limits statistical power relative to river n = 1207. This polymer-composition test is an independent line of evidence that does not depend on the fitting window — but the river-vs-ocean slope difference itself (Section 12.1.1) is separately confounded by different fitting windows (river 165–385 µm vs ocean 95–245 µm) and should be re-tested over a common overlapping window before that slope difference alone is attributed to source or transport.

12.5.3.1 Depth-stratified polymer composition (river surface/subsurface vs ocean)

River water has both sample_depth_general strata (700 surface, 507 subsurface particles). Ocean water does not: sample_depth_general is unrecorded for all 117 ocean-water particles in this study (0 with a recorded stratum), so an ocean depth split is not possible from this dataset – ocean is shown below as its own “depth not recorded” panel rather than assumed to be surface-only. The top-5 polymers by pooled river+ocean particle count set a common comparison basis across panels; every other polymer group is collapsed to “Other” so rare groups do not fragment the comparison.

Show the code

  dplyr::count(polymer_density_group, sort = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |>
  dplyr::pull(polymer_density_group)

m14_depth_panel_levels <- c("River water - surface", "River water - subsurface", "Ocean water - depth not recorded")

m14_depth_composition <- m14_particles |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    polymer_top5 = ifelse(polymer_density_group %in% m14_top5_polymers,

    polymer_top5 = factor(polymer_top5, levels = c(m14_top5_polymers, "Other")),
    panel = factor(paste(Matrix, Depth, sep = " - "), levels = m14_depth_panel_levels)

  dplyr::filter(!is.na(panel)) |>
  dplyr::count(panel, polymer_top5) |>
  dplyr::group_by(panel) |>

Interpretation. Comparing the two river panels isolates a within-matrix depth effect (same sampling program, same µFTIR workflow, same LOD window); comparing either river panel to the ocean panel still mixes a matrix effect with the unrecorded-depth limitation above. 36.8% buoyant fraction in ocean vs river’s surface/subsurface split (Section 12.5.3 table) is the more decision-relevant comparison than the full multi-polymer breakdown shown here, which is a descriptive, hypothesis-generating cross-tabulation. The within-river surface-vs-subsurface buoyancy comparison it motivates is tested formally below.

12.5.3.1.1 Formal test: are buoyant particles relatively more abundant at the river surface than subsurface?

Rationale: if buoyant (PP + PE) particles float toward and accumulate at the air-water interface, the river surface stratum should show a higher buoyant fraction than the subsurface stratum sampled at the same locations and times. This is a directional (one-sided) hypothesis, tested only within river water – ocean has no recorded depth stratum (Section 12.5.3.1 above), so it cannot be included.

Show the code

  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ci = list(stats::binom.test(n_buoyant, n)$conf.int),
    ci_low  = ci[1],
    ci_high = ci[2]
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(-ci)

nb_surf   <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n_buoyant[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "surface"]
nb_sub    <- river_depth_buoyant_fraction$n_buoyant[river_depth_buoyant_fraction$Depth == "subsurface"]
river_depth_2x2 <- table(river_depth_buoyant$Depth, river_depth_buoyant$is_buoyant)
river_depth_expected_min <- suppressWarnings(min(chisq.test(river_depth_2x2)$expected))

# One-sided two-proportion test: H1 = surface buoyant fraction > subsurface
# buoyant fraction. Falls back to a one-sided Fisher's exact test if any
# expected cell count is small (same threshold convention as Section 12.5.3's
# river-vs-ocean 2x2 test). river_depth_2x2 rows are (subsurface, surface) and
# columns are (not buoyant, buoyant), so a higher surface buoyant fraction
# implies odds ratio = (FALSE_sub * TRUE_surf) / (TRUE_sub * FALSE_surf) > 1
# -- alternative = "greater" is the correct one-sided direction for both tests.
river_depth_buoyancy_test <- if (river_depth_expected_min < 5) {
  fisher.test(river_depth_2x2, alternative = "greater")
} else {
  stats::prop.test(x = c(nb_surf, nb_sub), n = c(n_surf, n_sub), alternative = "greater")
}

cat(
  "Surface vs subsurface buoyant fraction, river water only:", river_depth_buoyancy_test$method,
  "-- one-sided H1: surface fraction > subsurface fraction -- p =", signif(river_depth_buoyancy_test$p.value, 4),
  "(min expected cell count =", round(river_depth_expected_min, 2), ")\n"
)
Surface vs subsurface buoyant fraction, river water only: 2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction -- one-sided H1: surface fraction > subsurface fraction -- p = 0.9985 (min expected cell count = 136.94 )

Interpretation. The river surface stratum’s buoyant fraction is 23.7% (n = 700) versus 31.6% at the subsurface (n = 507); the one-sided test above gives p = 0.998. This does not support the hypothesis – the observed direction is the opposite of what surface buoyant-enrichment would predict: the subsurface fraction is numerically higher than the surface fraction, though the 95% CIs above overlap substantially. Density-driven vertical sorting by buoyancy is not evident in this river dataset; the depth difference, if real, is more likely driven by something other than polymer buoyancy (e.g., local hydrodynamics, sampling time, or shape-dependent settling of non-buoyant fibers). This is a within-matrix, same-program, same-workflow comparison (unlike the river-vs-ocean buoyancy test in Section 12.5.3, which is additionally confounded by the ocean depth-recording gap noted above), so a significant result here would be comparatively strong evidence for local vertical sorting by buoyancy specifically.

15.1 Revised uncertainty interpretation

The main unresolved methodological uncertainties are now: (1) µFTIR objective and the marginal 50–100 µm detection zone, and (2) transport-induced PSD structural uncertainty described by Hoffman et al. (2026). The latter can affect absolute concentrations through the CF exponent, and may also affect relative comparisons when surface/subsurface samples, fibers/fragments, or buoyant/settling polymers are mixed in a pooled single-power-law fit. The sensitivity analyses above therefore replace the older conclusion that no further correction was warranted. The calibrated interpretation is that the Food Dilution pathway remains the dominant ERM in this screening assessment, while magnitude estimates should be read together with the slope-uncertainty, depth-stratified, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence diagnostics.

15.2 Modeling priorities

Hoffman et al. (2026) indicates that 3-D particle geometry and density inputs should be improved before investing effort in more complex settling-velocity equations. The current report follows that guardrail by adding polymer-resolved density and buoyancy flags, making δ and K explicit assumptions in the critical-size calculation, and retaining settling-based diagnostics as bias-level sensitivity checks rather than high-precision corrections. Future transport work should prioritize measured particle thickness, density, and shape-specific behavior; settling-equation refinements alone should not be expected to remove the dominant uncertainty.

15.3 Revised executive summary

This section restates the executive summary with the corrected numbers now that every matrix’s corrected and legacy sensitivity pipeline (Sections 5-14) has been computed, per SPEC 3b.

(a) Corrected Food Dilution RQ, after SPEC 1b. At a dev-scale iteration Monte Carlo budget (10 parameter-matrix replicates, 20000 slope draws), the corrected median Food Dilution HC5 RQ is 9.034 for river water (P(RQ>1) = 82.2%) and 3.278 for ocean water (median P(RQ>1) = 73.8%). Sediment is intentionally omitted from this headline figure (SPEC 1d): its nominal corrected Food Dilution HC5 RQ (153011.279, P(RQ>1) = 100%) is not a defensible risk estimate — Section 11.3.0/11.4.0 trace this to a placeholder exposure concentration (a per-liter water value reused as particles/kg) and a derived HC5 that fails the benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude — so it is excluded from the risk conclusion rather than reported alongside the river and ocean values.

(b) The prior (SPEC 1b-uncorrected) Food Dilution RQ was inflated by the volume-slope convention error. Reverting only a.v/a.sa/a.m to the legacy cumulative-as-differential convention (Appendix A), holding exposure and the length-slope alignment at their corrected values, the river-water Food Dilution HC5 median RQ becomes 40470174.826 — a 4479982.6-fold change relative to the corrected value of 9.034. This is the same mechanism and direction of error described in the SPEC 1b background (a mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation there estimates a ~4-6 million-fold effect at a = 0.76 vs. 1.68); the exact factor is a function of n_boot/n_mc and is expected to scale toward that estimate as the budget increases. No Food Dilution RQ figure in this report should be read as ~10^7 — that magnitude describes the pre-SPEC-1b (legacy) error being corrected here, not the corrected result.

(c) Tissue Translocation shift after both the length-slope and surface-area-slope fixes (revised, SPEC 3c). Reverting only the hazard-side length-slope alignment to its legacy cumulative-as-differential form, the river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 P(RQ>1) is 30.1%, versus 29.8% under the corrected alignment (Section 14.1). This is a material driver, but so is the surface-area slope: reverting a.v/a.sa/a.m together gives 69.6%, and isolating a.sa alone gives 69.1% — both far from the 29.8% corrected value, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted and therefore directly sensitive to the a.sa correction, unlike its (correctly) minimal sensitivity to the volume slope alone. A prior version of this narrative incorrectly called the volume/area effect on Tissue Translocation “essentially unchanged”; that claim is retracted here (Section 14.1 has the corrected attribution and the full one-at-a-time decomposition table, now covering both ERMs).

(d) Exposure as a single-slope-vs-piecewise bounding range (SPEC 2b). The production single-slope correction factor and its piecewise (dual-slope) bounding alternative are compared per matrix in Section 13.3 (Tables: single-slope vs. piecewise CF/EED, and the resulting Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ range). The single-slope CF remains the production default; the piecewise result is a labeled sensitivity bound quantifying structural (model-form) uncertainty in the unconstrained 1 µm-to-LOD sub-window, per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec.

(e) Sediment pathway excluded from the headline conclusion (SPEC 1d). The sediment (beach sand) risk characterization in Section 11 is retained in this report as a methods/illustrative demonstration only. Its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0), its hazard-side dose_unit = “kg” pathway was traced and found unit-consistent on its own terms with no discrete conversion bug identified (Section 11.4.0), and its sediment-specific ERM alignment slopes were independently verified correct and ruled out as the cause (Section 11.2, SPEC 1d-iv). The resulting sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails a rendered plausibility guard anchored on Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) by roughly eleven orders of magnitude. Until a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration is available, no sediment RQ in this report should be treated as a risk finding.

(f) Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment (SPEC 1e). Independent of the exposure-concentration problem in (e), Section 11.5 reframes sediment as an accumulating depositional sink in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so both bioaccessible exposure and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species become size-accessible) evolve over residence time (Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026). Any static sediment metric — including the illustrative Section 11.4 figures — is therefore a lower-bound snapshot, not an equilibrium value. Section 11.5.2 demonstrates this illustratively with a labeled, non-quantitative PSD-shift sensitivity showing the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 falling as the sediment PSD is shifted progressively finer; Section 11.5.4 adds a most-sensitive-species screen (sediment, plus a river/ocean companion) since individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal. This is a framework/sensitivity addition — it does not change point (e): sediment remains excluded from the headline risk conclusion.

Summary. Food Dilution remains the risk-dominant ERM relative to Tissue Translocation for river and ocean water in this screening assessment, consistent with the qualitative conclusion of the prior revision; the sediment pathway is excluded from this conclusion pending real concentration data (point (e) above). The magnitude of the Food Dilution RQ, however, depends materially on which of the three convention fixes above is applied, and the decomposition in Appendix A is intended to make that dependency auditable rather than implicit.

15.4 individual-species RCR — river/ocean companion screen

Section 11.5.4 added a most-sensitive-species screen for the sediment benthic dataset. This subsection completes SPEC 1e-iv’s companion request for the water compartments where exposure is quantitative (river, ocean): the single most sensitive species per ERM, plus the individual-species risk characterization ratio RCR = EED / lowest-species EC, reported as an early-warning companion to the community-HC5 RQ already characterized in Sections 7/12. This is placed here, after Section 15.3, because it is the first point in document execution order at which every matrix’s hazard (haz/haz_ocean) and EED (eed_boot/eed_boot_ocean) objects all exist together.

Appendices

The three appendices below hold convention-validation history, implementation-validation detail, and exploratory/non-quantitative sediment material that support the results above but are not needed to read them. Every number in this document – including here – is produced by the same live code as the main body; nothing here is retyped. SPEC-numbered labels below are preserved from docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md, which is the authoritative provenance record for each revision.

Appendix A: Convention-validation history

The differential-slope convention (length, area, volume, mass; Sections 5, 7) is the current basis throughout this report. This appendix quantifies the effect of each prior convention error that the SPEC 1/1b/3b/3c revisions corrected, and is why no number in the report body should be read as the pre-fix (≈10⁷, Food Dilution) legacy magnitude.

A.1 all-matrix CF before/after (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential)

Reruns the correction-factor convention check of Section 5.1 for all three matrices at once, comparing the legacy (cumulative slope passed as differential), corrected fit-only, and corrected structural-SD CF distributions side by side.

Show the code 
cf_case_summary <- function(matrix_label, cpsd_fit, combined_cf_current,
                            Lmin_use, Lmax_use, current_slope_draws, n = n_mc) {
  set.seed(4000 + nchar(matrix_label))
  cumulative_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_cpsd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_cpsd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  differential_fit_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_psd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  legacy_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = cumulative_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  corrected_fit_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = differential_fit_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_label,
    Case = c("Legacy cumulative slope passed as differential", "Corrected differential slope, fit SE only", "Corrected differential slope plus structural SD"),
    Slope_p50 = c(median(cumulative_draws), median(differential_fit_draws), median(current_slope_draws)),
    CF_p05 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.05), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.05), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.05)),
    CF_p50 = c(median(legacy_cf), median(corrected_fit_cf), median(combined_cf_current)),
    CF_p95 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.95), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.95), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.95))
  )
}

cf_before_after_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  cf_case_summary("River water", cpsd_fit_all, combined_cf, L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use, alpha),
  cf_case_summary("Sediment", cpsd_fit_sed_all, combined_cf_sed, L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed, alpha_sed),
  cf_case_summary("Ocean water", cpsd_fit_ocean_all, combined_cf_ocean, L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean, alpha_ocean)
)

knitr::kable(
  cf_before_after_all,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 1 all-matrix CF before/after: cumulative-vs-differential slope convention"
)

A.2 Food Dilution RQ decomposition (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential a.v/a.sa)

The Section 13 table above (SPEC 1, from the prior revision) shows that the length-slope convention fix changes the exposure correction factor. The volume/area-slope fix in this revision (SPEC 1b) is a separate, hazard-side-only effect: it does not touch correction_factor() or the EED at all, only the particle-trait alignment used inside pSSD++ (a.v.*, a.sa.*, a.m.*). To make that effect auditable, this section re-runs the pSSD++ hazard alignment and 1D risk characterization for each matrix with a “legacy” parameter set in which only a.v/a.sa/a.m are reverted to the pre-fix cumulative-slope values (legacy_cumulative_av_params(), R/mp_risk_utils.R) — holding the length slope, R.ave, exposure (EED), and everything else fixed — so the entire before/after RQ change in this table is attributable to the volume/area-slope convention alone.
